Mike identifies an improvement that management had not developed: staging parts by temperature and proposing interchangeable furnace tables. He understands the practical sequence of loading, waiting, handling, and preparing the next batch because he works directly with the process. Al responds by recognizing the idea, arranging engineering support, and planning to standardize it. The example shows that continuous improvement is not limited to analysts or senior managers. Employees closest to the work can see waste and propose workable changes, while management's role is to listen, evaluate, resource, and spread useful ideas.
Study instruction:
- "Interview an operator about one recurring delay. Ask what happens, where work waits, what is prepared in advance, and what change could remove the delay. Record how the idea would be tested."
Key point:
- Mike's practical knowledge revealed improvement opportunities in the actual work sequence.
- Create a route for frontline observations to be evaluated and implemented.
33. Q: Why did Al suggest rewarding Mike for improving heat-treat output?
A: Show answer
Al asks Bob to ensure Mike receives more money when the wage freeze is lifted. The recognition connects an improvement in constraint performance with the value the plant places on the employee's contribution. The story also shows Al giving Mike a more visible role and access to an industrial engineer so that his idea can be developed. Rewarding improvement can reinforce initiative, but a fair system should recognize sustainable throughput gains, quality, safety, and teamwork rather than raw volume alone. The chapter does not define a formal incentive scheme; the practical lesson is to acknowledge employees whose ideas materially improve the system.
Study instruction:
- "Design recognition criteria for a bottleneck improvement. Include verified throughput, quality, safety, repeatability, and contribution to other shifts."
Key point:
- Al intends to recognize Mike's measurable contribution and improvement idea.
- Recognition should reinforce sustainable system performance, not output at any cost.
34. Q: What did Bob discover about the unnecessary heat-treatment requirements?
A: Show answer
Bob reports that in three cases the plant itself, rather than engineering, had initiated the requirement for heat treatment. Several years earlier, a group had increased the cutting-tool bite on non-bottleneck machining centers from about one millimeter to three millimeters per pass to improve local processing efficiency. Removing more metal per pass made the material brittle, which then required heat treatment. The original change therefore increased the load on the heat-treat bottleneck. Bob realizes that the plant can return to the slower, previously approved processing method because the original efficiency change was its own option and an approved procedure already existed.
Study instruction:
- "Trace the causal chain from faster cutting to brittleness and additional heat treatment. Identify which process change created the downstream work."
Key point:
- Some heat-treat demand was created by the plant's own earlier efficiency initiative.
- Review upstream process changes for the secondary work they impose on constraints.
35. Q: Why could slowing down non-bottleneck machining reduce the load on heat-treat?
A: Show answer
The faster cutting method removed about three millimeters of metal per pass instead of roughly one millimeter. That increased local machining speed but made the metal brittle, creating a need for heat treatment. Because the affected machines were non-bottlenecks and had enough capacity to meet demand at the slower setting, the plant could return to the earlier process and avoid the additional heat-treatment requirement. Bob estimates that this would remove about twenty percent of the current furnace load. The example demonstrates that reducing the speed of a non-bottleneck can improve the whole system when it prevents unnecessary work at the constraint.
Study instruction:
- "Explain why the slower machining setting is feasible at a non-bottleneck but valuable to the plant. Verify the capacity assumption before recommending the change."
Key point:
- Slower upstream processing can reduce avoidable demand on the heat-treat constraint.
- Optimize the total process, not the speed of each individual operation.
36. Q: How does the chapter distinguish local efficiency from overall plant productivity?
A: Show answer
The plant previously increased the cutting-tool bite to make selected machining centers appear more efficient, but the faster process made parts brittle and created additional heat-treatment work. The affected machines were non-bottlenecks with enough capacity to operate more slowly and still meet demand. Reversing the speed increase would reduce local machining efficiency while removing about twenty percent of the current heat-treat load. The whole plant could therefore produce more useful output even though some machines processed more slowly. This is the chapter's clearest example of why maximizing each work center's utilization or speed can damage overall throughput.
Study instruction:
- "Choose an upstream efficiency initiative and trace its downstream effects on queues, rework, treatment, inspection, and constraint demand. Identify whether local speed improves the whole system."
Key point:
- Local efficiency can create extra work and reduce system productivity.
- Judge process changes by end-to-end throughput and delivery, not isolated utilization.
37. Q: Why was no new engineering change order required to reverse the earlier machining change?
A: Show answer
Bob explains that the faster cutting method had been initiated by the plant itself about five years earlier, and an approved procedure for the slower method remained on the books. Because the plant had originally chosen the change and could return to its existing approved procedure, Bob believed a new engineering change order was unnecessary. This is a specific fact of the chapter's scenario, not a universal rule for manufacturing change control. In a real operation, managers must verify document status, product specifications, customer requirements, and applicable authorization before changing a process. The lesson is to understand the origin and approval history of a process setting before assuming who must authorize its reversal.
Study instruction:
- "Review a process change history. Identify who initiated the change, which procedure is approved, whether it remains valid, and what authorization is required to reverse it."
Key point:
- The plant could revert because an approved earlier procedure remained available.
- Check the documented authority for a process change rather than assuming approval requirements.
38. Q: What is the relationship between upstream process decisions and downstream bottleneck demand?
A: Show answer
A process decision made at a non-bottleneck can increase the work that must later pass through a bottleneck. In the chapter, more aggressive cutting improved machining speed but made the metal brittle, creating additional heat-treat demand. Heat-treat then had to process parts that would not have needed that treatment under the earlier method. The decision shifted work downstream and increased pressure on the plant's constraint. This shows why process design must consider the entire route of a part, including secondary operations, rather than evaluate each operation independently. Changes that appear beneficial at one step may create more total work or longer delivery times later.
Study instruction:
- "For one product route, map how a change at an upstream work center affects every downstream operation. Highlight any added demand on a constrained process."
Key point:
- Upstream efficiency decisions can create downstream bottleneck work.
- Assess process changes across the full production route before approving them.
39. Q: How should a plant decide whether a non-bottleneck should run faster or slower?
A: Show answer
The decision should depend on whether the additional speed increases useful system output or merely creates more work for a constrained downstream operation. The chapter's faster cutting method increased local output but created brittleness and additional heat treatment. Since the machining centers were non-bottlenecks with spare capacity, slowing them down still allowed demand to be met while reducing heat-treat load. A manager should compare required demand, available capacity, quality consequences, downstream processing, and constraint utilization before selecting a speed. The aim is to maintain sufficient flow to the constraint without generating unnecessary work-in-process or avoidable processing.
Study instruction:
- "Evaluate a proposed speed increase using demand, non-bottleneck capacity, downstream effects, quality, and bottleneck load. State what evidence would justify retaining or reversing it."
Key point:
- The slower setting was acceptable because non-bottleneck capacity was sufficient.
- Set non-bottleneck pace to support the constraint and required demand, not to maximize local speed.
40. Q: How do the chapter's staffing, equipment, and process changes work together?
A: Show answer
The plant's response is a coordinated package. Dedicated teams reduce waiting at heat-treat and the NCX-10. Older machines add an alternative route for selected NCX-10 work. An outside vendor takes some heat-treat overflow. Mike's pre-staging and proposed interchangeable tables reduce preparation and changeover time. Finally, reversing the unnecessary faster cutting method removes about twenty percent of the heat-treat load. Each measure attacks a different source of constraint loss or demand. The chapter therefore does not present a single magic solution; it shows that throughput can improve through several mutually reinforcing changes to capacity, availability, scheduling, and upstream process design.
Study instruction:
- "Create a cause-and-action matrix linking each observed loss or excess load to the chapter's corresponding intervention. Identify dependencies between the actions."
Key point:
- The response combines protecting capacity, adding alternatives, and reducing unnecessary constraint demand.
- A constraint strategy should address both lost capacity and avoidable workload.
41. Q: What is the value of using bottleneck output to predict shipment capability?
A: Show answer
Ralph suggests that the plant might use bottleneck output to predict when an order can ship. The idea follows from the constraint's role in limiting the system's flow: if the plant knows what work must pass through the bottleneck, how much capacity is available, and which orders have priority, it can form a more realistic view of completion timing. Such a forecast would need accurate actual cycle and queue data, reliable routing information, and visibility of downstream completion requirements. The chapter presents this as a possibility Ralph wants to explore, not as a completed scheduling system. It points toward using constraint performance as a basis for more credible delivery promises.
Study instruction:
- "Design a simple order forecast using required bottleneck work, available constraint time, queue sequence, and downstream lead time. Identify what data must be validated first."
Key point:
- Ralph sees bottleneck measurements as a possible basis for shipment prediction.
- Reliable delivery estimates begin with accurate knowledge of constraint workload and capacity.
42. Q: What operational indicators would help monitor whether the chapter's improvements are working?
A: Show answer
Useful indicators follow directly from the losses and changes described: actual furnace in-and-out times, elapsed time between heats, post-cycle waiting, changeover duration, NCX-10 setup response time, constraint idle periods, parts processed by shift, and completed shipments. Managers should also monitor overdue-order priorities, queue size, quality results, and whether work moved to older machines or an outside vendor returns on time and to specification. No single measure is sufficient. For example, more furnace loads are not beneficial if quality falls or urgent orders are displaced. Indicators should reveal whether constraint time is being protected and whether that protection results in better system flow.
Study instruction:
- "Build a shift-level dashboard with definitions for each measure, data owner, review frequency, and an exception threshold that triggers investigation."
Key point:
- The chapter highlights actual times, constraint output, shift differences, and shipment results.
- Measure both constraint performance and the system outcomes it is meant to improve.
43. Q: What risks arise when operators try to increase furnace utilization by changing batch composition?
A: Show answer
Grouping parts by temperature can reduce setup delay, but it must not cause incompatible parts to be treated together, override order priorities, or compromise identification and traceability. Mike's example works because the primary overdue parts and the additional retaining rings require the same 1,200-degree cycle. A manager applying the idea should verify each part's approved treatment specification, batch limits, loading arrangement, and quality requirements. The chapter shows Mike maintaining the priority system; that discipline is essential. Better furnace fill is valuable only when it preserves the required process and does not delay higher-priority work.
Study instruction:
- "Review a proposed mixed load. Verify temperature compatibility, treatment specification, capacity, order priority, and traceability before approving it."
Key point:
- Batch consolidation is useful only when the parts share a valid treatment cycle and priority rules are respected.
- Do not trade process conformity or delivery priority for higher apparent utilization.
44. Q: How should a plant standardize an improvement discovered on one shift?
A: Show answer
The chapter's response to Mike's idea is to move him to day shift temporarily and pair him with an industrial engineer to write the procedure formally. Standardization should capture the steps that produced the improvement, specify the equipment and materials required, define who performs each action, and explain how the method is handed over across shifts. It should also include safety and quality checks and a way to report exceptions. After documentation, supervisors can train all shifts, observe actual use, and revise the procedure if trials reveal problems. The goal is not to freeze learning but to make a proven method repeatable and improvable.
Study instruction:
- "Create a rollout plan from one-shift discovery to plant-wide use: validate, document, train, trial on each shift, monitor, and revise."
Key point:
- Mike's practice is to be formalized for round-the-clock use.
- An improvement is not fully implemented until it can be repeated across shifts.
45. Q: What management mistake would occur if the plant continued rewarding every work center for maximum local efficiency?
A: Show answer
The plant could encourage decisions that increase the output or utilization of non-bottlenecks while creating excess work for the constraint. The earlier cutting-speed change is the example: local machining became faster, but the material became brittle and required heat treatment. That additional load made the furnace constraint harder to manage. A system that rewards each area independently may therefore produce more intermediate inventory, more downstream processing, and fewer finished shipments. Management should connect performance measures to flow and throughput, while still preserving quality, safety, and cost discipline. The chapter challenges the assumption that a busy or fast work center is necessarily helping the plant.
Study instruction:
- "Identify a local performance target and test whether improving it could increase downstream workload, waiting, or constraint demand. Propose a system-level companion measure."
Key point:
- Local efficiency incentives helped create work that burdened the bottleneck.
- Performance measures should reward contribution to system results, not isolated activity.
46. Q: What decision principles can be extracted from Al's response to the heat-treat problem?
A: Show answer
Al first validates the seriousness of the lost time, then protects the constraint with dedicated coverage, redirects resources from areas with excess capacity, and authorizes additional internal and external capacity where useful. He also recognizes a frontline improvement and arranges for it to be standardized. Finally, he supports removing work that the plant itself had unnecessarily created through an earlier process change. These actions combine diagnosis, immediate protection, capacity relief, employee involvement, and root-cause removal. The chapter's management lesson is to address both symptoms and causes: ensure the bottleneck is ready now while changing the system so that avoidable demand does not continue to return.
Study instruction:
- "Summarize Al's actions in sequence and classify each as diagnosis, protection, capacity addition, standardization, or root-cause reduction."
Key point:
- Al responds through a sequence of operational changes rather than a single isolated fix.
- Effective constraint management combines immediate controls with structural improvement.
47. Q: How can a plant tell whether an improvement has increased throughput rather than merely moved work or cost?
A: Show answer
The plant should compare completed shipments and order performance before and after the change, while checking whether work has simply accumulated elsewhere. The chapter begins with a gap between projected and actual shipments and then changes staffing, equipment use, subcontracting, and process settings to improve flow. A valid assessment should therefore track constraint output, downstream completion, overdue orders, quality, total labor and supplier costs, and the number of orders actually shipped. More parts entering heat-treat or a higher utilization figure is not enough by itself. The result matters when the system converts the improvement into completed, saleable output.
Study instruction:
- "Define a before-and-after review for one intervention. Include shipments, lead time, queue movement, quality, and incremental cost so that displaced work is not mistaken for a gain."
Key point:
- The chapter links bottleneck improvements to the plant's ability to ship more orders.
- Confirm system-level results rather than relying only on activity at the improved work center.
48. Q: What is the chapter's central lesson about improving a production system?
A: Show answer
The chapter shows that improving a plant requires identifying where the flow is constrained, measuring what actually happens there, and protecting the constraint from avoidable waiting. The heat-treat and NCX-10 examples show the value of dedicated support, while the older machines and outside vendor provide alternative capacity. Mike's work demonstrates that advance preparation, compatible batching, and faster changeovers can release more constraint time. The earlier cutting-speed decision shows that local efficiency can create unnecessary downstream demand, and that slowing a non-bottleneck may improve the whole plant. The combined lesson is to manage the flow of completed products, not to maximize the apparent efficiency of every individual operation.
Study instruction:
- "Explain how measurement, constraint protection, capacity relief, frontline improvement, and upstream demand reduction fit into one coherent operating strategy."
Key point:
- The chapter moves from discovering hidden constraint losses to redesigning the system around throughput.
- Improve the whole flow by protecting constraints and eliminating work that does not contribute to useful output.
Rows: 48
Table 22
Constraint Migration, Production Flow, and Continuous Improvement
1. Q: What operational achievement is celebrated at the plant, and why is it significant?
A: Show answer
The team celebrates a new monthly shipping record: 57 customer orders worth approximately $3 million, compared with the previous best of 31 orders worth about $2 million. Stacey also reports a 12 percent net reduction in work-in-process inventory over the month. The significance is not simply that more goods left the plant. The result suggests that recent changes to the way the constraint is managed have improved the plant's ability to convert its resources into completed customer orders while carrying less unfinished stock. The chapter presents this as evidence of progress, while the later discovery of shortages shows that a strong result is not proof that the system has become permanently stable.
Study instruction:
- "Compare the old and new shipment records, then explain why shipment volume and WIP must be reviewed together rather than separately."
Key point:
- The plant shipped more orders and higher shipment value while WIP declined.
- An improvement is evidence to investigate and sustain, not a reason to stop monitoring.
2. Q: What do the figures of 31 orders and 57 orders reveal about the plant's performance?
A: Show answer
The figures show a substantial increase in the number of customer orders shipped in a month. The plant moved from a prior record of 31 orders to 57, an increase of 26 orders, or roughly 84 percent relative to the previous record. The reported shipment value also rose from about $2 million to approximately $3 million. These figures indicate a marked change in delivery output and commercial activity. They do not, by themselves, establish profitability, margin, cash collection, or the cost of producing the orders. A sound performance review therefore treats the figures as operational evidence and checks them against quality, delivery reliability, inventory, costs, and customer outcomes.
Study instruction:
- "Calculate the percentage increase in orders and identify at least three financial or operational measures that shipment value alone cannot establish."
Key point:
- The order count increased by about 84 percent over the previous record.
- Shipment value is not the same as profit, cash received, or sustainable operating performance.
3. Q: Why should shipment value not be confused with profit?
A: Show answer
The toast refers to approximately $3 million of product shipments, but shipment value is a measure of sales or dispatch activity, not a complete profit calculation. Profit also depends on the costs and accounting treatment associated with the products, the timing of revenue recognition, returns, discounts, warranty obligations, overheads, and other relevant items. The chapter's celebration is understandable because more customer orders are being completed, but a manager should not infer that the plant has earned $3 million in profit or cash. The more disciplined conclusion is that the plant has improved its shipment performance. Financial results must be assessed through the appropriate income statement, cost information, and cash records.
Study instruction:
- "Rewrite the celebration statement as a management report that distinguishes shipment value, recognized revenue, cash collection, and profit."
Key point:
- The $3 million figure describes approximate shipment value in the story.
- Financial conclusions require cost, revenue-recognition, and cash-flow evidence.
4. Q: What does the 12 percent decline in work-in-process inventory indicate?
A: Show answer
A 12 percent net decline in work-in-process inventory means that the value or quantity of unfinished production held between process stages has fallen over the reported period, according to Stacey's calculation. In the narrative, the reduction is visible operationally: employees can approach the assembly line without squeezing between large stacks and bins. Lower WIP can indicate that materials are moving through the system with less accumulation and that production is being released more in line with the system's ability to complete work. It may also reduce handling, congestion, search time, and the risk of parts becoming difficult to locate. The decline is encouraging, but it must be interpreted alongside shortages, throughput, due dates, and service performance.
Study instruction:
- "Explain how lower WIP can improve flow, and list the additional measures needed before concluding that the plant has improved overall."
Key point:
- The decline is consistent with reduced accumulation and better flow.
- Low inventory is not automatically good if essential parts are missing and orders cannot be completed.
5. Q: Why is it useful to evaluate throughput and WIP together?
A: Show answer
Throughput and WIP provide complementary views of a production system. Throughput reflects the rate at which the system generates completed output that can satisfy customer demand, while WIP represents work that has entered production but is not yet complete. If completed shipments rise while WIP falls, as in the chapter, the combination is stronger evidence of improved flow than either measure alone. If WIP falls because work is not being released, however, throughput may also fall. Conversely, high output accompanied by rapidly rising WIP may indicate that work is entering the system faster than it can be completed. Managers should therefore examine the direction and relationship of both measures, together with operating expense and delivery reliability.
Study instruction:
- "Construct four simple cases showing high or low throughput alongside rising or falling WIP, and explain what each combination might mean."
Key point:
- Throughput measures completed system output; WIP measures unfinished work in the system.
- Interpret the measures jointly and investigate the cause of each movement.
6. Q: Does a record month prove that the plant's operational problems have been solved?
A: Show answer
No. The record month demonstrates meaningful progress, but the later report of missing non-bottleneck parts reveals a new weakness. The plant's earlier constraint-management actions increased the output of heat-treat and the NCX-10, and the higher flow placed more demand on other work centers. A resource that previously had spare capacity may now be unable to meet the demand created by the improved upstream flow. This is why operational improvement must be treated as a continuing process. A good month is a result to validate, not a guarantee that the system will perform equally well under a changed product mix, demand level, or capacity profile.
Study instruction:
- "Identify which evidence in the chapter supports the record-month celebration and which later evidence shows that the improvement was incomplete."
Key point:
- A performance record confirms progress at a point in time.
- A changed system can expose a different constraint, so monitoring must continue.
7. Q: How does the customer feedback from Bill Peach and Johnny Jons reinforce the operational results?
A: Show answer
Peach reports that Johnny Jons is pleased because the plant has recently delivered a number of late customer orders. This feedback connects internal production changes to an outcome that matters outside the factory: customers are receiving orders that had previously been delayed. It also shows that operational performance is noticed by commercial and senior-management stakeholders. The praise is not merely personal recognition for Al; it is evidence that improved production flow can restore confidence and improve the plant's service reputation. Managers should nevertheless verify the pattern over time through on-time delivery, overdue-order aging, promise-date adherence, and customer complaints rather than relying on a single favorable conversation.
Study instruction:
- "Translate the feedback into measurable customer-service indicators that could be monitored over several reporting periods."
Key point:
- The customer-facing effect of improvement is more reliable delivery of overdue orders.
- Anecdotal praise should be corroborated with recurring delivery and service data.
8. Q: Why does the plant's backlog matter when evaluating the new production performance?
A: Show answer
The chapter notes that the backlog is declining as throughput rises. A backlog represents customer work that has been accepted or promised but has not yet been completed, depending on the plant's definition. A falling backlog can indicate that completed output is catching up with incoming demand and that overdue orders are being cleared. However, backlog reduction must be interpreted carefully: it could also result from cancellations, reduced order intake, or changes in order classification. The useful operational question is whether the plant is completing real customer demand more consistently and reducing overdue commitments without creating new shortages or quality problems. The backlog should be segmented by age, product, customer priority, and reason for delay.
Study instruction:
- "Design a backlog review that distinguishes completed orders, newly received orders, cancellations, overdue work, and orders blocked by missing components."
Key point:
- The reported decline in backlog is consistent with improved throughput.
- Backlog movement needs a clear definition and reconciliation to actual customer demand.
9. Q: What is a bottleneck in the context of this chapter?
A: Show answer
A bottleneck is a resource or stage whose available capacity is insufficient relative to the demand placed on it, thereby restricting the rate at which the system can complete work. Earlier in the story, heat-treat and the NCX-10 were known constraints. The team took steps to protect and improve their output. The later shortage of green-tagged parts suggests that other resources may now be limiting the flow of components to final assembly. A bottleneck is therefore not simply a machine that is busy, a department with a long queue, or a resource that employees dislike. It is a system constraint demonstrated by the relationship between required workload, effective capacity, and the effect on completed orders.
Study instruction:
- "For one work center, estimate required workload and practical capacity, then explain whether the evidence indicates a true system constraint."
Key point:
- A bottleneck has demand that exceeds or critically consumes its effective capacity.
- Its importance is determined by its effect on total system output, not by local busyness alone.
10. Q: What does it mean that bottlenecks have spread or migrated?
A: Show answer
The phrase describes a change in where the system's limiting capacity is located. After the plant improves the output of existing bottlenecks, more work can flow to other stages. Those stages may then receive more demand than they can process, creating one or more new constraints. The original bottleneck may still exist, but it may no longer be the only factor preventing completion of orders. Constraint migration is a predictable possibility in a system whose resources have different capacities and whose demand changes as improvements take effect. The chapter's central operational warning is that a successful intervention changes the conditions being managed, so yesterday's constraint map may no longer describe today's production system.
Study instruction:
- "Draw a before-and-after process map showing how relieving one constraint can move the limiting point to another resource."
Key point:
- Improving one constraint can expose another constraint downstream or elsewhere in the routing network.
- The constraint map must be refreshed when flow and demand change.
11. Q: Why can making an existing bottleneck more productive create a new bottleneck elsewhere?
A: Show answer
When a constraint produces more output, additional components are released into the rest of the production network. Those components require processing at other work centers before they can be assembled into finished products. If a receiving work center has insufficient capacity, its queue grows or parts become unavailable when assembly needs them. In the chapter, higher throughput and a declining backlog increase the demand placed on resources beyond heat-treat and the NCX-10. A previously non-constraining work center may cross the point at which its required workload exceeds its effective capacity. The improvement has not necessarily caused waste; it has changed the load profile and exposed a capacity limitation that was less visible before.
Study instruction:
- "Trace one component from an improved bottleneck to final assembly and identify where additional workload could exceed available capacity."
Key point:
- Relieving a constraint changes the workload imposed on other resources.
- A new bottleneck can be an indirect consequence of successful improvement.
12. Q: What does it mean for a work center to be loaded above 100 percent of capacity?
A: Show answer
In the discussion, Al recognizes that a new bottleneck may exist if demand on another work center has risen above 100 percent of its capacity. This is a practical warning that the required processing load is greater than the resource can complete in the available time. The calculation should use effective capacity rather than an unrealistic theoretical maximum: planned operating hours, staffing, setup, maintenance, downtime, yield, and product-specific processing times all matter. A workload above capacity cannot be cleared sustainably by simply urging employees to work faster. It will tend to create queues, late parts, overtime pressure, expediting, or missed assembly requirements unless capacity, routing, demand, or priorities are changed.
Study instruction:
- "Build a workload-to-capacity calculation for a hypothetical work center and identify which assumptions would need verification."
Key point:
- A sustained load above effective capacity is a strong bottleneck warning.
- Capacity analysis must include real operating losses and the actual product mix.
13. Q: What symptoms in the chapter suggest that new constraints may have appeared?
A: Show answer
Stacey reports that final assembly is waiting for some non-bottleneck parts as well as the familiar bottleneck parts. In the DBD-50 example, 17 of 172 required part types are missing, although only one missing item is red-tagged. The known red-tagged part has already completed heat-treat, while most of the missing green-tagged parts remain unavailable. Purchasing has not identified a supplier problem, and the parts do not require outside contractor processing. These symptoms point toward an internal capacity or scheduling issue beyond the original bottlenecks. They do not yet prove exactly which resource is constrained; they justify a focused investigation using part, routing, workload, and queue data.
Study instruction:
- "Separate the chapter's observed facts from Stacey's hypothesis, then identify what additional evidence would confirm a new bottleneck."
Key point:
- The missing green-tagged parts are the key new symptom.
- Symptoms indicate where to investigate; they do not alone identify the exact constrained resource.
14. Q: What does the DBD-50 order example reveal about material availability?
A: Show answer
The plant needs to build an order for 200 DBD-50 units, and the product requires 172 different part types. At the time described, 17 of those part types are missing, which is approximately 9.9 percent of the distinct part types required. Only one of the missing types is red-tagged; the other 16 are green-tagged. This is operationally important because an order can be blocked by a small number of missing components even when most required materials are present. The example also shows why managers must look beyond the parts traditionally treated as critical. A component's absence can stop final assembly regardless of whether the component itself passed through a previously identified bottleneck.
Study instruction:
- "Calculate the missing-part percentage and explain why a parts-completeness measure should be based on the bill of materials for each order."
Key point:
- Seventeen of 172 required part types are missing, or about 9.9 percent.
- A small number of missing components can prevent completion of the entire order.
15. Q: Why is it important that only one of the 17 missing DBD-50 part types is red-tagged?
A: Show answer
The color distinction shows that the shortage is not confined to the parts already recognized as bottleneck-related. The plant's priority system identifies one missing red-tagged item, while 16 missing items are green-tagged. This challenges the assumption that the bottleneck parts will be the last components to arrive at assembly and that non-bottleneck parts will be available in time. The result suggests that the system's release, scheduling, or capacity assumptions for green-tagged components need to be examined. It does not prove that the tags themselves caused the shortage. The colors are a signal to compare planned priority with actual part availability and routing performance.
Study instruction:
- "Review a sample of order shortages and classify each missing component by its current priority designation and actual constraint exposure."
Key point:
- The shortage pattern includes many components outside the known bottleneck category.
- A priority classification must be tested against actual completion performance.
16. Q: What does the chapter establish about the red-tagged part that passed through heat-treat?
A: Show answer
The one missing red-tagged part came out of heat-treat on Thursday and was ready by Friday morning. That detail indicates that the known bottleneck-related component completed the heat-treat stage relatively promptly in this case. The order is still incomplete because the other missing components have not arrived. The observation therefore shifts attention from the old constraint alone to the broader component flow required for assembly. It does not show that heat-treat is no longer a bottleneck for all products or periods. It shows that clearing the red-tagged part is insufficient if other required parts are delayed elsewhere in their routings.
Study instruction:
- "Use the DBD-50 case to explain why completing a bottleneck operation does not guarantee that the finished order can be assembled."
Key point:
- The red-tagged part was ready after heat-treat, but the order remained blocked.
- An order is complete only when all required components and operations are available.
17. Q: Why does the absence of a purchasing problem matter in Stacey's diagnosis?
A: Show answer
Stacey rules out a known purchasing problem and notes that none of the missing parts require processing by outside contractors. This narrows the investigation toward internal production capacity, routing, scheduling, or material-flow issues. It is a useful diagnostic step because not every shortage has the same cause. A supplier delay calls for vendor follow-up, alternative sourcing, or procurement action; an internal capacity constraint calls for analysis of work centers, workload, sequencing, and available hours. Eliminating external explanations does not automatically prove that a new bottleneck exists, but it prevents the team from applying a procurement solution to a problem that appears to originate within the plant.
Study instruction:
- "Create a cause tree for a missing component that distinguishes supplier, subcontractor, internal processing, inventory-record, and scheduling causes."
Key point:
- The chapter rules out supplier and outside-contractor explanations for the reported parts.
- Correct diagnosis matters because different shortage causes require different interventions.
18. Q: Why should managers trace missing parts through their routings?
A: Show answer
A routing identifies the sequence of operations and work centers required to produce a part. By mapping each missing component to its routing, managers can see which resources it uses, where it is currently waiting, and whether the same work center appears repeatedly among late parts. If many unrelated parts share a common operation, that operation becomes a stronger candidate for investigation. If shortages are scattered across unrelated routings, the cause may instead involve release timing, priority rules, data quality, or several constraints. Stacey's requested analysis of affected parts and routings is therefore essential to moving from a general impression of shortages to a testable explanation of the system's behavior.
Study instruction:
- "Take five missing components and map their operation sequences; identify shared work centers and distinguish common-cause patterns from isolated delays."
Key point:
- Routing data links a shortage to the resources that process the part.
- Repeated appearances of one work center across late routings can reveal a common constraint.
19. Q: Why are listings of parts queued for final assembly useful diagnostic evidence?
A: Show answer
A queue of components awaiting final assembly makes visible the gap between what assembly needs and what upstream production has supplied. Reviewing the listing can identify which part numbers are missing, how many are required, how long they have been waiting, and which products or customer orders are affected. The queue is a downstream symptom, not necessarily the location of the root cause. Managers must trace each part backward through its routing and compare the actual stage reached with the planned schedule. A queue report becomes much more useful when it includes due dates, quantities, priority, work-center history, and shortage frequency rather than only a static list of part numbers.
Study instruction:
- "Specify the fields that should appear in an assembly-shortage report and explain how each field helps diagnose the source of delay."
Key point:
- Assembly shortage listings reveal the immediate completion problem.
- Root-cause analysis requires tracing each missing part upstream through its routing.
20. Q: How can product mix create a new bottleneck even when total plant demand appears manageable?
A: Show answer
Different products consume different amounts of time at each work center and follow different routings. A plant may have enough total hours in aggregate yet lack sufficient capacity at a particular operation that is heavily used by the current mix. The DBD-50 order illustrates the importance of product-specific part requirements: it depends on 172 distinct part types, each with its own processing path. If demand shifts toward products that use a particular machine or operation intensively, that resource can become overloaded even when the total number of orders seems reasonable. Capacity planning should therefore translate the order mix into operation-level workload rather than rely only on units, order counts, or total sales value.
Study instruction:
- "Compare two hypothetical product mixes with equal order counts but different routings, and calculate the workload imposed on each critical work center."
Key point:
- Capacity depends on the work content and routing mix, not just the number of orders.
- Aggregate plant demand can conceal a shortage at a specific operation.
21. Q: What is protective capacity, and why does it matter after a bottleneck is improved?
A: Show answer
Protective capacity is the ability of non-constraint resources to provide enough spare capacity to support the flow required by the constraint and the rest of the system. In a production network, not every resource should be expected to operate at maximum utilization all the time. Some unused capacity is necessary to absorb variation, recover from disruptions, and ensure that parts arrive when needed. After heat-treat and the NCX-10 become more productive, downstream and supporting work centers face a greater flow of work. If they have too little protective capacity, the plant can exchange one visible bottleneck for several new shortages. The chapter's emerging problem illustrates why spare capacity at non-constraints is operationally valuable rather than automatically wasteful.
Study instruction:
- "Identify where spare capacity is needed in a multi-stage routing and explain how it protects the completion rate of the whole system."
Key point:
- Non-constraint capacity supports flow and absorbs variability.
- Maximizing local utilization everywhere can make the system less reliable.
22. Q: How do the actions taken to exploit the original bottlenecks relate to the new shortage problem?
A: Show answer
The team had placed quality control in front of bottlenecks, trained employees to give special care to bottleneck parts, activated three machines to supplement the NCX-10, changed lunch rules, assigned certain people to work only at bottlenecks, increased batch sizes entering heat-treat, and introduced a new priority system. These actions were intended to protect or increase the output of the known constraints. As those constraints became more productive, more work flowed through the system and increased demand elsewhere. The new shortages do not automatically invalidate the earlier actions. They show that constraint-focused improvements must be followed by a review of the entire routing network and the capacity of supporting resources.
Study instruction:
- "For each action listed in the chapter, state which original constraint problem it was intended to address and what new workload consequence might follow."
Key point:
- The earlier actions focused on increasing or protecting heat-treat and NCX-10 output.
- Successful constraint exploitation changes the load on other resources and requires renewed analysis.
23. Q: Why was quality control placed in front of the bottlenecks?
A: Show answer
A defective part that consumes scarce bottleneck time wastes capacity that the system cannot easily recover. Inspecting quality before a part enters a constraint helps prevent avoidable rework or scrap from using the resource's limited productive time. The chapter lists this as one of the measures introduced after the earlier bottleneck analysis. The principle is that scarce capacity should be reserved for work that has a reasonable chance of becoming usable output. Inspection itself must be designed carefully: it should detect meaningful defects without creating excessive delay or becoming a new queue. The quality gate should therefore be risk-based, timely, and connected to clear acceptance criteria and corrective action.
Study instruction:
- "Design a pre-constraint quality check that defines defect criteria, responsible personnel, recording requirements, and escalation for rejected parts."
Key point:
- Defective work should be detected before it consumes scarce constraint capacity.
- Inspection must protect flow without creating unnecessary delay or another bottleneck.
24. Q: Why did the plant activate three additional machines to supplement the NCX-10?
A: Show answer
The chapter identifies the activation of three machines as an action intended to supplement the NCX-10, one of the known bottlenecks. Adding or reactivating capacity can increase the amount of work that passes through a constrained operation, provided the machines are suitable, staffed, maintained, and supplied with work. The broader lesson is that capacity additions should be evaluated by their effect on system throughput rather than by machine count alone. Additional machines may shift workload to other stages, require new skills or maintenance, or create setup and scheduling complexity. The later green-part shortages show why a capacity intervention must be followed by system-wide monitoring.
Study instruction:
- "Assess a proposed machine-capacity addition by considering effective hours, quality, staffing, routing compatibility, downstream capacity, and impact on completed orders."
Key point:
- The three machines were activated to supplement the NCX-10 constraint.
- Additional capacity at one stage can increase demand and expose limits elsewhere.
25. Q: Why were certain employees assigned to work only at the bottlenecks?
A: Show answer
Dedicated attention can reduce interruptions, task switching, and delays at a resource whose output determines the system's completion rate. Employees assigned to bottleneck work can develop familiarity with the operation, maintain readiness, and avoid being pulled away for lower-priority tasks. The chapter lists this staffing arrangement among the plant's recent measures. However, specialization needs clear coverage, training, relief arrangements, and workload balance. A dedicated assignment should not create dependence on one person or allow other essential operations to be neglected. Managers should measure whether the arrangement improves constraint uptime and completed output, not simply whether the assigned employees appear busy.
Study instruction:
- "Evaluate a dedicated-operator arrangement using uptime, output, quality, skill coverage, absence risk, and downstream completion measures."
Key point:
- Protecting constraint time can improve the system's output.
- Dedicated staffing still requires resilience, cross-training, and evidence of actual performance benefit.
26. Q: What operational purpose might the revised lunch rules serve?
A: Show answer
The chapter includes new lunch rules among the measures introduced to improve the use of bottleneck resources. The likely operational purpose is to prevent the constraint from being unavailable at the same time as essential coverage disappears, thereby smoothing production across the working period. A schedule can stagger breaks, maintain qualified coverage, and reduce avoidable idle time. The story does not specify the exact rule or schedule, so no particular break arrangement should be assumed. Any policy change must also comply with employment law, safety requirements, collective agreements, and organizational rules. Its effectiveness should be evaluated through constraint availability, output, fatigue, safety, and employee feedback.
Study instruction:
- "Draft a compliant coverage plan for a critical work center and identify the operating data needed to assess whether it improves availability."
Key point:
- Break scheduling can protect the availability of a critical resource.
- The exact policy is not stated and must not be invented; legal and safety requirements remain applicable.
27. Q: Why might increasing batch sizes entering heat-treat improve one constraint but create other problems?
A: Show answer
Larger batches can reduce the frequency of setups or transfers and may help keep a constrained process productively occupied. The chapter says the plant increased batch sizes going into heat-treat as part of its effort to improve the original constraint. However, larger batches can also increase waiting time before a batch is complete, create more WIP, delay parts needed by assembly, and reduce flexibility when product priorities change. The best batch size is therefore not necessarily the largest possible. Managers must weigh setup efficiency against flow time, inventory, due-date responsiveness, and the risk that one delayed batch holds up several orders.
Study instruction:
- "Compare two batch-size policies using setup time, average waiting time, WIP, and the effect on customer-order completion."
Key point:
- Larger batches may improve constraint efficiency by reducing setup frequency.
- Batch decisions must also account for flow time, WIP, and responsiveness.
28. Q: What is the role of the red-tag and green-tag priority system in the chapter?
A: Show answer
Al explains that the plant introduced a priority system using red and green tags, with red associated in the discussion with bottleneck parts and green with other parts. The system is intended to help employees recognize which components need special attention and coordinate work around the constraints. Jonah immediately asks about this new system, signaling that the design and consequences of the rules deserve scrutiny. The chapter does not provide a full specification of the tag logic, so it would be inaccurate to invent detailed release rules, timing formulas, or exact meanings beyond the stated distinction. The practical lesson is that a visual priority mechanism must reflect current system conditions and be checked against actual material availability.
Study instruction:
- "Document the actual meaning, trigger, owner, and update rule for each priority tag before assessing whether the system is working."
Key point:
- The chapter distinguishes red-tagged bottleneck parts from green-tagged non-bottleneck parts.
- A priority system must be understood precisely and validated against actual production flow.
29. Q: Why might a priority system fail to ensure that all components reach final assembly in time?
A: Show answer
A priority label can direct attention, but it cannot create capacity at an overloaded work center or guarantee that every operation in a routing will finish on schedule. The DBD-50 example shows a red-tagged part becoming available while 16 green-tagged part types remain missing. If the green-tagged parts require work at resources that are now overloaded, the priority system may be protecting the old constraints while overlooking the new limits. A system can also fail if tags are applied incorrectly, not updated, ignored, or disconnected from realistic due dates and routing information. Priority rules must be supported by capacity planning, release control, reliable data, and escalation for blocked components.
Study instruction:
- "Test a priority rule against a sample of completed and late orders; identify cases where the tag did not predict actual availability."
Key point:
- Priority labels coordinate attention but do not substitute for capacity.
- A tag system must adapt when constraints change and must be validated with outcome data.
30. Q: Why is it dangerous to assume that non-bottleneck parts will always arrive before bottleneck parts?
A: Show answer
That assumption may have been reasonable under the earlier operating conditions, but the chapter shows that it is no longer reliable. As the known bottlenecks become more productive, other resources may receive enough additional work to become constraints themselves. A green-tagged component can then be delayed even while the red-tagged component passes through its critical operation. The practical danger is that planners may continue releasing, scheduling, or expediting work based on an obsolete picture of capacity. The result can be incomplete kits, idle assembly labor, missed customer dates, and excess work in process. Managers should base material-readiness assumptions on current routing performance rather than historical labels.
Study instruction:
- "Identify one planning assumption that was valid before a capacity improvement and explain how you would retest it afterward."
Key point:
- A component's old priority category does not guarantee its current completion time.
- Historical assumptions must be revalidated after changes to system capacity.
31. Q: How can managers distinguish a true new bottleneck from an isolated late part?
A: Show answer
A single late part may result from a one-time defect, incorrect inventory record, missed transaction, unusual setup, employee absence, or a local scheduling mistake. A true new bottleneck is more likely when multiple parts repeatedly queue at the same resource, the required workload exceeds effective capacity, and the delays materially restrict final assembly or customer shipments. Managers should examine the frequency and duration of shortages, the number of products and orders affected, common routings, work-center queues, utilization, downtime, and actual processing hours. The chapter asks Stacey to collect exactly which parts are missing, how many, which products are affected, which routings they use, and how often shortages occur. That evidence helps distinguish a recurring capacity problem from isolated exceptions.
Study instruction:
- "Create a diagnostic checklist that compares one-off exceptions with recurring, shared-work-center patterns."
Key point:
- A true constraint is demonstrated by repeated system impact and capacity evidence.
- One missing component is a symptom to investigate, not conclusive proof of a bottleneck.
32. Q: What information does Al ask Stacey to collect, and why is each item important?
A: Show answer
Al asks for the exact parts involved, the quantities missing, the products affected, the routings used, and how often the parts are missing. Part identifiers make the issue traceable; quantities show the scale of the shortage; affected products connect component delays to customer orders; routings reveal shared work centers; and frequency distinguishes recurring patterns from isolated incidents. A useful extension is to add due dates, queue age, planned and actual operation times, current location, scrap or rework history, and the time the shortage was first detected. This turns a general warning into a structured operational dataset that can support root-cause analysis and a defensible decision about where capacity or scheduling changes are needed.
Study instruction:
- "Build a shortage-analysis template using every requested field and add only fields that would materially improve diagnosis."
Key point:
- The requested data links missing parts to product impact, routing, and recurrence.
- Specific evidence is required before changing capacity or priority rules.
33. Q: Why does Stacey need to know how often each part is missing?
A: Show answer
Frequency helps distinguish a persistent pattern from an unusual event. A component that is late once may have experienced a temporary disruption; a component that is missing in a high proportion of orders may point to a recurring routing, capacity, scheduling, quality, or inventory-control weakness. Frequency should be interpreted alongside severity and duration. A rare shortage of a component that blocks a high-value or urgent order may still be critical, while frequent minor delays may be recoverable without stopping assembly. A useful analysis records the number of orders requiring the part, the number of orders in which it was unavailable when needed, the delay duration, and the downstream effect.
Study instruction:
- "Calculate a shortage rate for several parts and rank them by both recurrence and impact on completed orders."
Key point:
- Frequency helps reveal recurring problems but must be combined with severity and delay duration.
- The most frequent shortage is not automatically the most important system constraint.
34. Q: Why should the investigation identify every affected product, not just the missing part numbers?
A: Show answer
The same missing part can affect many products, while one product can be delayed by several different components. Product-level analysis reveals the commercial and operational reach of the shortage. It helps managers identify whether the issue is concentrated in a particular product family, customer order, or set of routings. It also supports decisions about sequencing, substitution where technically permitted, customer communication, and the allocation of scarce capacity. In the DBD-50 example, the 200-unit order is blocked by a set of missing components. Knowing only the part numbers would not show whether other products are affected by the same resources or whether the shortage is isolated to that order.
Study instruction:
- "Map missing components to all open orders that require them and identify the total customer demand exposed to each shortage."
Key point:
- Part-level data must be connected to product and order-level consequences.
- The same resource problem may affect several products and customers.
35. Q: How should managers use work-center workload data to confirm a new constraint?
A: Show answer
Managers should convert the open and expected production requirements into operation-level workload, then compare that workload with the work center's effective capacity over the relevant time horizon. The analysis should use realistic processing times, setups, staffing, shifts, downtime, maintenance, yield, and product mix. It should also distinguish work already waiting from work that has not yet been released. A queue that grows over several periods while the resource is operating near its practical limit is stronger evidence than a one-time high utilization figure. The result should be checked against missing-part histories and the impact on final assembly. This combines capacity arithmetic with observable system consequences.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a weekly workload-versus-capacity schedule for one candidate work center and reconcile its forecast with actual queue growth."
Key point:
- Capacity confirmation requires both quantitative workload analysis and evidence of system impact.
- Use effective capacity and a defined planning horizon rather than theoretical machine capacity.
36. Q: Why is a plant-wide view necessary when diagnosing production shortages?
A: Show answer
A local manager may see a busy machine, a growing queue, or a shortage in one department and try to maximize that department's output. But production is a linked network: a change at one stage alters the flow and workload at others. The chapter demonstrates this interdependence when improvements to heat-treat and the NCX-10 are followed by shortages of green-tagged parts. A plant-wide view asks how each resource contributes to completed customer orders, where parts wait, and which constraint currently limits total flow. It prevents local optimization, such as producing more components that cannot be assembled, from being mistaken for genuine system improvement.
Study instruction:
- "Draw the full routing network for a product and identify how a local output increase could affect queues and capacity elsewhere."
Key point:
- Production resources are interdependent.
- The right objective is better system flow and completed orders, not maximum output at every individual work center.
37. Q: What is the difference between keeping a bottleneck busy and improving total plant performance?
A: Show answer
Keeping a bottleneck busy can be valuable because idle time at a true constraint may reduce the system's ability to complete orders. However, a resource can appear productive while producing items that are not needed, are defective, or cannot move through the rest of the system. Total plant performance depends on converting constrained capacity into useful finished output. The chapter's record shipments and lower WIP suggest that the earlier changes improved system results, but the new missing parts warn against judging success solely by activity at the original bottlenecks. Managers should link constraint utilization to assembly readiness, completed shipments, backlog, quality, and inventory rather than reward isolated machine activity.
Study instruction:
- "Compare a local utilization report with a system-level performance report and identify the decisions each could lead a manager to make."
Key point:
- Busy resources do not automatically produce more completed customer orders.
- Constraint performance must be evaluated through its contribution to system throughput.
38. Q: Why can maximizing utilization at every work center be harmful?
A: Show answer
If every non-bottleneck resource is pushed to produce continuously, it may release more work than the rest of the system can absorb. That can increase queues, WIP, handling, and confusion without increasing completed shipments. A non-constraint should have enough capacity to support the system and absorb variation, but it does not need to produce simply to maintain a high utilization percentage. The chapter's reduction in WIP is a favorable sign, while the later shortages show that flow still depends on balanced capacity and timely supply of all required components. The management objective is to synchronize work with the system's needs, not to make every machine appear fully occupied.
Study instruction:
- "Identify an example where producing more at a non-constraint would increase WIP but not increase the number of finished orders."
Key point:
- Local utilization is not the same as system productivity.
- Uncontrolled release of work can create excess WIP and obscure the actual constraint.
39. Q: How should managers interpret the combination of falling WIP and new component shortages?
A: Show answer
The two observations are not contradictory. Falling WIP may indicate that excessive piles of unfinished work have been reduced and that some parts are flowing more smoothly. At the same time, a new resource may be unable to supply a particular set of components when assembly needs them. The plant can therefore have less total WIP but still experience critical shortages in specific routings. Aggregate inventory figures can hide the location, composition, and readiness of stock. Managers should supplement total WIP with part-level availability, order-kitting completeness, queue age, and shortage frequency. The goal is not simply to minimize inventory but to maintain the right materials in the right quantities at the right stages.
Study instruction:
- "Design a report that pairs total WIP trends with component-level shortage and order-readiness indicators."
Key point:
- An aggregate WIP reduction can coexist with shortages of specific critical components.
- Inventory must be evaluated by location, part, readiness, and effect on customer orders.
40. Q: What does the chapter teach about the timing of a new bottleneck review?
A: Show answer
The review should be triggered when evidence shows that the operating system has changed enough to invalidate previous assumptions. In the chapter, higher throughput, declining backlog, and new shortages of green-tagged parts create that trigger. Managers should not wait for a prolonged collapse in shipments before investigating. At the same time, they should avoid declaring a new constraint based on one unexplained shortage. A disciplined review uses early warning indicators such as repeated missing components, growing queues, increasing workload-to-capacity ratios, and assembly starvation. After a major constraint intervention, a scheduled review is especially useful because the workload distribution is likely to have changed.
Study instruction:
- "Set early-warning thresholds for recurring shortages, queue growth, and workload-to-capacity ratios, distinguishing alerts from confirmed diagnoses."
Key point:
- Reassess constraints when flow patterns or shortage evidence change.
- Early investigation is preferable to waiting until customer shipments deteriorate.
41. Q: Does finding a new bottleneck mean that the plant must start the entire improvement process from zero?
A: Show answer
No. The plant should preserve what has been learned and reassess the current system rather than discard all prior improvements. The original measures may still be protecting heat-treat and the NCX-10 effectively. The new task is to identify which additional resources now limit the flow, determine whether the existing constraint remains binding, and adjust priorities and capacity accordingly. The chapter captures Al's frustration at the thought of repeating the process, but the underlying lesson is continuous improvement: each successful change alters the system and may reveal the next limitation. The team should update its diagnosis, not assume that all previous work was wasted.
Study instruction:
- "Separate the practices that should remain in place from the assumptions that must be retested after a new constraint is suspected."
Key point:
- A new constraint calls for an updated diagnosis, not an automatic restart from zero.
- Preserve effective controls while adapting the plan to the current system.
42. Q: Why does Jonah ask specifically about the new priority system?
A: Show answer
Jonah's question indicates that the priority system is a significant part of the plant's changed operating method and needs to be understood before he can assess the symptoms. A new rule may affect which parts are released, how work is sequenced, what employees expedite, and how the plant responds to competing demands. If the rules are inconsistent with current constraints or are applied without accurate routing and capacity information, they may contribute to shortages or hide them. The chapter does not disclose Jonah's final judgment, so it would be premature to say that he has identified the priority system as the cause. His question is a diagnostic prompt to examine the logic and actual effects of the new control.
Study instruction:
- "Explain the priority system to a reviewer in terms of purpose, triggers, ownership, data inputs, exceptions, and observed results."
Key point:
- A changed priority rule can materially influence production flow.
- Jonah's question begins an examination; it is not yet a finding that the system is faulty.
43. Q: How can visual priority controls be kept reliable as constraints change?
A: Show answer
A visual control remains useful only if its categories reflect current operating reality and employees understand how to act on them. Managers should define the meaning of each tag, the conditions for applying or changing it, who is authorized to update it, and how exceptions are escalated. The system should be reconciled to current routings, open orders, capacity information, and material availability. Periodic sampling can test whether tagged parts are actually arriving in the expected sequence and whether untagged or lower-priority parts are becoming chronic shortages. When the constraint moves, the visual rules may need revision. The control should guide decisions, not become a fixed ritual that employees follow after its assumptions have expired.
Study instruction:
- "Write a control procedure for updating priority tags after a constraint review, including authorization, communication, and audit trail."
Key point:
- Visual controls must be maintained as live representations of current priorities.
- A tag without clear ownership, update rules, and outcome testing can become misleading.
44. Q: What is the relationship between constraint management and final assembly readiness?
A: Show answer
Final assembly can complete an order only when the required components are available in the necessary quantities and have passed their required operations. Improving a single constrained operation may speed up one subset of parts, but the order remains blocked if another required component is missing. The DBD-50 case makes this dependency visible: the red-tagged part is ready, yet the 16 missing green-tagged part types still prevent the order from being fully assembled. Assembly readiness is therefore a system outcome. It depends on coordinated material flow across all routings, accurate inventory records, timely operations, and the availability of every required component.
Study instruction:
- "Create an order-readiness checklist that verifies every required part, quantity, operation status, quality status, and shortage owner before assembly starts."
Key point:
- Final assembly depends on the complete set of required components, not one critical part alone.
- Constraint management must protect end-to-end order readiness.
45. Q: How should a manager respond when assembly labor is available but components are missing?
A: Show answer
The manager should first identify exactly which components are missing and whether the shortage is physical, transactional, quality-related, or caused by an incomplete operation. The team should trace each part through its routing, establish the current location and queue, assess the effect on the order, and determine whether the delay is isolated or recurring. Assembly labor should not be left waiting without a plan, but moving people to unrelated work or changing priorities must be coordinated with production control. The manager should communicate a realistic recovery estimate, assign an owner to each shortage, and escalate common-work-center patterns. Expediting should be selective and should not merely transfer disruption to other orders.
Study instruction:
- "Work through a simulated assembly shortage and prepare an action log showing verification, owner, next operation, recovery estimate, and escalation."
Key point:
- Verify the cause and status of a missing part before expediting it.
- Recovery actions should protect the whole schedule rather than create hidden disruption elsewhere.
46. Q: What risks arise when a plant responds to every shortage by expediting the affected part?
A: Show answer
Uncontrolled expediting can repeatedly interrupt planned work, create frequent setups, displace other orders, and make the schedule less predictable. If many parts are expedited simultaneously, employees may receive conflicting priorities and the plant may lose visibility over the real constraint. Expediting a component may also fail if the resource is already operating above capacity. A more disciplined response distinguishes urgent customer impact from routine delay, confirms the root cause, and directs scarce capacity toward the work that best supports system throughput and commitments. The red/green experience in the chapter is a reminder that priority rules must be coherent across the production network, not simply a collection of individual emergency requests.
Study instruction:
- "Compare a controlled priority queue with an ad hoc expediting process and identify the risks of each."
Key point:
- Expediting can help with a genuine urgent exception but is not a substitute for capacity analysis.
- Too many competing priorities can destabilize the production schedule.
47. Q: How can management tell whether a capacity intervention has improved the system rather than shifted the problem?
A: Show answer
Management should compare results before and after the intervention across the whole production chain. Relevant indicators include completed shipments, throughput, backlog, WIP, order lead time, on-time delivery, quality, queue age, work-center load, and missing-part frequency. The plant's record shipments and 12 percent WIP reduction are favorable signals, while the new green-part shortages are a warning that the improvement may have exposed another limit. A complete review asks whether the original constraint's output increased, whether downstream operations absorbed the additional work, and whether the customer experienced better completion and delivery. If the queue simply moves to another work center, the system has changed but not necessarily improved sustainably.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a before-and-after scorecard that includes at least one system outcome, one inventory measure, one customer measure, and one constraint indicator."
Key point:
- Measure the effect across the whole system, not only at the resource that was changed.
- A queue that moves downstream may indicate constraint migration rather than full resolution.
48. Q: What role should cross-functional coordination play in the response to the new shortages?
A: Show answer
The problem crosses several functions. Production control needs accurate priorities and routing data; work-center supervisors know actual queues and capacity; quality personnel identify rejected or reworked parts; inventory staff verify recorded and physical balances; purchasing confirms external supply; and assembly teams identify the components that prevent order completion. Stacey's discussion with Al combines production data with procurement checks, and Al assigns her a structured investigation while he contacts Jonah. A coordinated response prevents each function from optimizing its own activity or blaming another department without evidence. The team should use one shared shortage record, common definitions, named owners, and a regular review of unresolved items.
Study instruction:
- "Assign roles for a cross-functional shortage review and specify what evidence each function must contribute."
Key point:
- The shortage diagnosis requires information from multiple functions.
- Shared data and clear ownership reduce fragmented responses and blame.
49. Q: Why is it important to separate evidence from assumptions during the bottleneck investigation?
A: Show answer
The chapter contains observed facts and hypotheses. Observed facts include the 17 missing DBD-50 part types, the one red-tagged item, the ready date of that item, the absence of known purchasing and subcontracting problems, and the recent rise in throughput. Stacey hypothesizes that one or more new bottlenecks have appeared; Al considers whether demand on other work centers has exceeded capacity. These are plausible explanations, but the exact constrained resources have not yet been confirmed. A disciplined manager records what is known, what is inferred, and what evidence is still required. This prevents premature investment, unnecessary schedule changes, and misdirected corrective action.
Study instruction:
- "Create a three-column investigation log labelled confirmed fact, working hypothesis, and evidence still required for the DBD-50 shortage."
Key point:
- The new bottleneck is a hypothesis to test, not a fully established diagnosis at this point in the story.
- Explicitly separating facts and assumptions improves decision quality.
50. Q: How should the plant use expert advice when the operating system changes?
A: Show answer
Al contacts Jonah after describing the symptoms and the changes made since Jonah's previous visit. Jonah asks about the actions taken and specifically about the new priority system, then says he may need to visit the plant again. This shows the value of bringing an experienced external or specialist perspective to a changed operating problem. The plant should provide complete facts, not only a preferred explanation, and should be prepared to show actual routings, queues, workload, capacity, and priority rules. Expert advice is most useful when it tests the team's assumptions and improves its diagnosis. It does not remove management's responsibility to validate the analysis and implement changes carefully.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a concise briefing for an operations adviser that includes the problem statement, evidence, actions already taken, and unresolved questions."
Key point:
- Expert review can challenge assumptions and interpret changing system conditions.
- The plant remains responsible for accurate evidence and controlled implementation.
51. Q: What does the chapter suggest about the relationship between continuous improvement and management attention?
A: Show answer
Continuous improvement requires managers to remain attentive after a successful change. The team has achieved record shipments and lower WIP, yet Stacey identifies a new pattern of missing parts. The response is not to celebrate indefinitely or to assume that the previous solution will work forever. It is to gather new data, examine the changed workload, and consult Jonah. This is a recurring management cycle: observe system performance, identify a constraint, improve it, monitor the consequences, and reassess the system. Improvements are not isolated projects with a permanent endpoint. They change the environment in which the next set of decisions must be made.
Study instruction:
- "Describe a recurring improvement cycle for the plant and identify the measures that should trigger another review."
Key point:
- Every significant improvement changes the conditions for future management.
- Continuous improvement depends on observation, learning, and repeated reassessment.
52. Q: How can a plant avoid confusing inventory reduction with inventory elimination?
A: Show answer
The chapter celebrates a reduction in WIP, not the elimination of all inventory.
