The actual reduction depends on release rules, processing times, product mix, replenishment reliability, and how batches overlap, so managers should verify the result from observed inventory rather than assume every category will fall by exactly half.
Study instruction:
- "Compare work-in-process quantities before and after a controlled batch-size change, using consistent product and time-period definitions."
Key point:
- Smaller batches can reduce the amount of work accumulated inside the plant.
- Measure actual inventory changes instead of treating a 50% reduction as automatic.
5. Q: Why does lower work-in-process release cash for other uses?
A: Show answer
Work-in-process represents money already committed to materials and conversion activities that have not yet become saleable finished goods. When less material is tied up between operations, the organization may need less working capital to sustain the same production flow. Stacey connects lower work-in-process and lower overall inventory with reduced cash pressure. This is a working-capital benefit from reducing the amount and duration of capital tied up in production; it is not necessarily an immediate cash receipt or accounting profit by itself. The financial effect should be assessed alongside purchasing terms, supplier payment timing, production stability, and finished-goods requirements.
Study instruction:
- "Map the cash path from purchasing raw material through work-in-process to shipment and identify where inventory reduction releases working capital."
Key point:
- Less inventory can reduce the cash committed to the operating cycle.
- A working-capital release is distinct from revenue or profit recognition.
6. Q: Why must supplier delivery frequency change if the plant wants to reduce total inventory?
A: Show answer
Reducing internal batch sizes alone may lower work-in-process but leave excessive raw-material inventory if suppliers continue delivering large quantities infrequently. To reduce inventory across the supply chain, purchasing must negotiate more frequent deliveries in smaller quantities while preserving reliable availability. This requires examining supplier capacity, transport economics, minimum order quantities, lead times, quality arrangements, and administrative effort. The chapter presents supplier cooperation as a necessary condition for realizing the full inventory and cash-flow benefit, not as an automatic consequence of changing shop-floor batch sizes.
Study instruction:
- "Select a high-volume input and compare current delivery quantity and frequency with a feasible smaller-and-more-frequent replenishment pattern."
Key point:
- Internal batch reduction does not automatically reduce incoming inventory.
- Purchasing and suppliers must coordinate replenishment changes.
7. Q: What commercial issues should purchasing examine before asking suppliers for smaller, more frequent deliveries?
A: Show answer
Purchasing should assess whether suppliers can meet the proposed cadence without creating shortages, quality deterioration, excessive freight cost, or unstable prices. It should review contractual minimums, order-processing charges, transport capacity, supplier production cycles, delivery reliability, and the cost of holding inventory on either side. The plant should identify which materials are critical to bottleneck schedules and which can tolerate more flexible replenishment. Negotiations should be based on total supply-chain economics rather than simply transferring storage or transport costs to the vendor. Revised arrangements should define quantities, delivery windows, escalation procedures, and performance measures.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a supplier discussion sheet showing current and proposed order quantities, delivery frequency, service expectations, and total-cost implications."
Key point:
- Supplier agreements must support reliable flow, not just smaller purchase orders.
- Evaluate total cost and risk across both supplier and plant operations.
8. Q: What are the four elements of the time a part spends inside the plant?
A: Show answer
The chapter divides total elapsed time into setup time, process time, queue time, and wait time. Setup time is the period when the part waits while a resource prepares to work on it. Process time is the period when the resource actually changes the part into a more valuable form. Queue time is the period the part waits in line because the required resource is busy with earlier work. Wait time is the period the part waits for another part needed to complete an assembly. These categories distinguish productive transformation from delays caused by capacity, sequencing, and synchronization.
Study instruction:
- "Draw a timeline for one part and classify each interval as setup, process, queue, or wait."
Key point:
- Total elapsed time consists of four distinct elements.
- Only process time directly transforms the part.
9. Q: How is setup time different from process time?
A: Show answer
Setup time is associated with preparing a resource for a particular job, such as changing tools, fixtures, settings, or other conditions needed before work can begin. During this interval the part is not yet being transformed by the operation. Process time is the interval in which the resource performs the operation that changes the part into a more valuable form. Separating the two prevents managers from confusing preparation activity with value-adding transformation. It also helps identify whether setup reduction is increasing system output or merely creating more available time at a resource that is not limiting throughput.
Study instruction:
- "Observe an operation and record the point at which preparation ends and actual transformation of the part begins."
Key point:
- Setup prepares the resource; process changes the part.
- A reduction in setup time is valuable only in relation to the system's constraint and demand.
10. Q: How is queue time different from wait time?
A: Show answer
Queue time occurs when a part is ready for a resource but cannot be processed because that resource is occupied with work ahead of it. Wait time occurs when a part is not waiting for a busy machine but for another required part so that assembly can take place. The distinction matters because the causes differ. A queue in front of a bottleneck reflects constrained capacity and accumulated workload. A wait before assembly may reflect an imbalance between the timing of bottleneck-produced components and components made at non-bottlenecks. Treating both simply as machine delay can conceal the actual cause of long lead times.
Study instruction:
- "For one product, identify a queue delay before a resource and a synchronization delay before assembly."
Key point:
- Queue is a resource-capacity delay; wait is a parts-synchronization delay.
- Different delay causes require different improvement responses.
11. Q: Why can setup and process time represent only a small part of total elapsed time?
A: Show answer
A part may spend relatively little time being prepared and physically processed but much longer waiting for a resource or for another component. The chapter emphasizes that queue and wait can account for most of the time between material entering the plant and the finished product leaving it. Improving the speed of an operation may therefore have limited effect on customer lead time if large queues and assembly waits remain. Managers need to examine the complete elapsed-time path, not just the time recorded against machine operations.
Study instruction:
- "Calculate the percentage of total elapsed time represented by each of the four time elements for a representative product."
Key point:
- Machine processing is not the same as total production lead time.
- Waiting can dominate elapsed time even when processing is efficient.
12. Q: Why is queue time especially important for parts that pass through a bottleneck?
A: Show answer
A bottleneck has less available capacity than the workload requires, so work accumulates in front of it. Parts waiting for that constrained resource experience queue time while earlier jobs consume its limited capacity. The longer the queue, the longer parts remain inside the plant before continuing toward completion. Because the bottleneck governs the pace at which the system can complete work, its queue influences downstream production and customer orders. Reducing unnecessary releases and protecting the bottleneck's productive time are central to controlling this delay.
Study instruction:
- "Inspect the queue before a known constraint and identify how much waiting is caused by workload, priorities, or premature material release."
Key point:
- Bottleneck capacity creates the dominant queue for affected parts.
- Queue control must protect and synchronize work around the constraint.
13. Q: Why is wait time especially important for parts made at non-bottlenecks?
A: Show answer
A part produced at a non-bottleneck may finish its own operation quickly but still be unable to enter assembly until the matching component from a bottleneck arrives. It therefore waits for synchronization rather than for the non-bottleneck machine to become free. Producing large quantities early can increase the pile of components that are not yet usable in a finished product. The chapter explains that wait time is dominant for parts that pass only through non-bottlenecks because they often depend on components whose timing is governed by the bottleneck.
Study instruction:
- "Map the component requirements for one assembly and compare the completion times of bottleneck and non-bottleneck components."
Key point:
- A component can be finished and still not be ready for assembly.
- Non-bottleneck production should be synchronized with constraint-driven demand.
14. Q: How do bottlenecks influence both inventory and throughput?
A: Show answer
Bottlenecks determine the pace at which the system converts available work into completed output. They also influence when other components are needed and how long parts remain in queues or wait for assembly. If upstream non-bottlenecks produce far ahead of the constraint, inventory accumulates without increasing finished output. If materials arrive too late at the bottleneck, the system may lose throughput. Thus the constraint affects both the rate of flow and the amount of inventory required or accumulated around that flow. Inventory and throughput should be managed as connected system outcomes.
Study instruction:
- "Trace how the constraint's schedule determines release, component timing, work-in-process, and finished output for one product route."
Key point:
- The constraint governs system pace and strongly shapes inventory accumulation.
- More local production does not necessarily create more finished throughput.
15. Q: Why does the chapter challenge reliance on the economical batch quantity formula?
A: Show answer
The plant has been using an economical batch quantity formula, but Jonah says that the formula rests on assumptions that are flawed for the situation being discussed. The chapter does not enumerate those assumptions in detail; it uses the criticism to prompt a practical test of halving current batch sizes. A formula based on local setup or ordering economics may not capture the effects of bottlenecks, queue time, wait time, inventory, and customer lead time. A calculated optimum should therefore be tested against actual system constraints and performance.
Study instruction:
- "List the assumptions embedded in the batch-sizing method used in your operation and test whether they reflect current constraints and flow behavior."
Key point:
- A mathematically convenient batch quantity may not optimize system performance.
- Validate batch policies against actual flow, constraints, and outcomes.
16. Q: How can smaller batches reduce queue time and wait time?
A: Show answer
Smaller batches allow portions of a job to move to the next operation without waiting for the entire original quantity to finish. This can reduce the amount of work ahead of a resource and make matching components available for assembly sooner. The chapter reasons that halving batch size can reduce the time needed to process a batch and, in turn, reduce queue and wait. The actual reduction depends on routing, transfer rules, resource capacity, setup behavior, and synchronization. The principle is to shorten the time work is trapped in large lots rather than assume every delay will fall in exact proportion.
Study instruction:
- "Run a before-and-after trial that records queue and wait intervals separately instead of relying only on total lead time."
Key point:
- Smaller transfer quantities can move work forward sooner.
- Measure the impact on each delay in the real production route.
17. Q: How does reduced time inside the plant affect production lead time?
A: Show answer
Production lead time is the elapsed time required for work to move through the plant from the relevant starting point to shipment readiness. If smaller batches reduce the time parts spend in queues and waiting for assembly, the total time inside the plant can contract. The chapter links this shorter internal elapsed time to faster order turnaround. Managers should define the start and end points consistently, because plant-floor lead time may differ from the customer's full order-to-delivery time, which can include order entry, engineering, procurement, transport, and other activities.
Study instruction:
- "Define the exact start and end events for the plant lead-time measure and keep those definitions unchanged during the trial."
Key point:
- Less waiting inside production can shorten order turnaround.
- Lead-time measures need consistent boundaries for valid comparisons.
18. Q: Why does faster flow matter more than simply keeping every machine busy?
A: Show answer
The chapter's reasoning is system-oriented: the objective is to complete and ship valuable products, not to maximize the activity of every individual resource. A non-bottleneck can have idle time without reducing system output because its capacity exceeds the constraint's capacity. Keeping it busy by producing excess batches may create inventory and longer waits rather than additional finished throughput. Faster flow means work moves in a coordinated way toward completion, with the bottleneck protected and other resources synchronized to its needs. Local utilization is not a reliable substitute for system performance.
Study instruction:
- "Compare a local machine-utilization report with system throughput, work-in-process, and delivery performance for the same period."
Key point:
- High utilization at every resource is not the system's primary objective.
- Coordinated flow can outperform maximum local activity.
19. Q: What does the rule that an hour lost at a bottleneck is an hour lost for the entire system mean?
A: Show answer
A bottleneck limits the rate at which the whole system can produce. If it loses an hour of productive time and that time cannot be recovered, the system loses an hour of its constrained production opportunity. Other resources may have spare capacity, but they cannot fully replace the missing bottleneck output. This is why protecting the constraint from avoidable downtime, missing materials, poor scheduling, and unnecessary setup disruption is important. The rule focuses attention on the resource whose time determines system throughput rather than treating every machine hour as equally consequential.
Study instruction:
- "Identify a recent bottleneck interruption and estimate its effect on completed system output, not only the affected machine's idle time."
Key point:
- Bottleneck time has system-wide value.
- Protecting constraint availability is more important than indiscriminate utilization.
20. Q: What does the rule that an hour saved at a non-bottleneck is a mirage mean?
A: Show answer
An hour saved at a non-bottleneck may appear to improve efficiency, but it does not increase system throughput when the bottleneck remains limiting and the non-bottleneck already has sufficient idle capacity. In the chapter, smaller batches create more setups at non-bottlenecks, yet those setups consume time that would otherwise have been idle. Reducing those setups would save local time without creating more completed products. The saving is a mirage when it is counted as a system benefit even though it does not improve constraint output or another meaningful system result.
Study instruction:
- "For a non-bottleneck improvement proposal, state which system measure will change and demonstrate why the change is not merely local time saved."
Key point:
- Local time saved is not automatically system capacity gained.
- Judge non-bottleneck efficiency by its effect on the whole flow.
21. Q: Why can additional setups at a non-bottleneck be acceptable after material release is synchronized?
A: Show answer
The chapter explains that the plant has begun withholding materials from the floor until bottlenecks are ready for them. As a result, non-bottlenecks have idle time. Smaller batches may require more frequent setups, but those setups can use part of the idle capacity without reducing system output, provided the non-bottleneck still completes required work in time for the constraint and assembly. This does not mean setups are costless or should be ignored. It means setup frequency should be evaluated against available slack and system flow rather than automatically minimized at every machine.
Study instruction:
- "Compare expected setup workload with non-bottleneck available capacity and confirm that required components will still be ready on schedule."
Key point:
- More setups can be absorbed when sufficient non-bottleneck idle capacity exists.
- Acceptability depends on capacity, timing, and synchronization.
22. Q: How should managers respond to concerns that smaller batches will increase direct labor and setup costs?
A: Show answer
Managers should acknowledge the local cost concern, then compare it with system-level effects. More setups may consume additional labor or machine preparation time, but if they use otherwise idle non-bottleneck capacity they may not reduce throughput. Lower work-in-process, shorter lead time, faster delivery, and improved sales opportunity may outweigh incremental setup effort. The analysis should quantify both sides rather than dismiss cost concerns. It should also check whether any affected setup occurs at a bottleneck, because additional constraint setup time has a different and potentially serious system consequence.
Study instruction:
- "Build a before-and-after cost and capacity comparison that separates bottleneck setups from non-bottleneck setups."
Key point:
- Assess setup cost in relation to available capacity and system results.
- Never assume a setup at a bottleneck has the same consequence as one at a non-bottleneck.
23. Q: Does halving batch size always halve total production lead time?
A: Show answer
No. The chapter presents an approximate improvement logic: smaller batches reduce batch processing duration and can reduce queue and wait, leading to a substantial contraction in total elapsed time. The result is not a universal mathematical guarantee. Actual lead time also depends on setup duration, transfer rules, product routing, bottleneck availability, demand mix, material supply, assembly synchronization, and scheduling discipline. Some time elements may not respond proportionally to batch size. Managers should treat the halving example as a testable operating hypothesis, establish a baseline, run a controlled trial, and compare observed outcomes.
Study instruction:
- "Identify which elapsed-time components are expected to change proportionally and which require separate measurement."
Key point:
- The chapter's halving logic is a practical hypothesis, not a universal law.
- Validate lead-time changes with operational data.
24. Q: How should a plant select an initial smaller batch size without destabilizing production?
A: Show answer
A practical starting point is to test the proposed half-size batch on selected products or routes where the constraint schedule and material availability are understood. Managers should confirm that the smaller quantity can be processed, transferred, tracked, and assembled without creating confusion or shortages. They should monitor setup frequency, queue levels, work-in-process, bottleneck starvation, delivery performance, and quality. If the trial reveals a problem, the team can adjust the quantity or operating rules before expanding. The recommendation is specific, but sound implementation requires controlled observation and operational discipline.
Study instruction:
- "Design a limited pilot with a defined product scope, baseline measures, owners, review dates, and criteria for expansion or adjustment."
Key point:
- Start with a measurable trial rather than an uncontrolled plant-wide change.
- Protect the bottleneck and assembly schedule throughout the test.
25. Q: Which operating measures should be monitored during a batch-size reduction trial?
A: Show answer
The plant should monitor work-in-process quantity and value, raw-material and finished-goods inventory, setup frequency and duration, process time, queue time, wait time, total production lead time, bottleneck utilization and interruptions, throughput, on-time shipment, and cash tied up in inventory. These measures reveal whether the change improves flow or merely shifts cost and delay elsewhere. Results should be segmented by product or route where necessary because an overall average can conceal a problem on a particular family. A baseline and consistent definitions are essential for meaningful comparison.
Study instruction:
- "Create a before-and-after scorecard with operational, delivery, and working-capital measures and define each metric precisely."
Key point:
- Measure the full chain of effects, not just batch size or setup count.
- Segment results where product routes and constraints differ.
26. Q: Why should inventory reductions be checked across raw materials, work-in-process, and finished goods?
A: Show answer
The chapter discusses reducing work-in-process and, with supplier cooperation, potentially reducing broader inventory. Looking only at work-in-process could hide a transfer of stock into raw materials or finished goods. Purchasing may continue to order large quantities while production releases smaller lots, or the plant may build finished goods ahead of demand to keep machines occupied. A complete inventory review checks whether the total amount of cash tied up is falling and whether service levels remain reliable. It also distinguishes a genuine reduction from reclassification or movement of stock between categories.
Study instruction:
- "Reconcile inventory balances by category before and after the trial and investigate any category that rises while another falls."
Key point:
- Inventory improvement must be assessed across the full stock cycle.
- A reduction in one category can be offset by accumulation elsewhere.
27. Q: How can purchasing and operations coordinate the new batch policy?
A: Show answer
Operations should communicate the production sequence, constraint requirements, and quantities needed at each stage. Purchasing should translate those requirements into supplier schedules, delivery quantities, and replenishment agreements. Inventory control can monitor on-hand stock, expected receipts, and consumption, while suppliers confirm capacity and delivery commitments. A shared schedule reduces the risk that operations release smaller batches but purchasing continues to replenish in large, disconnected lots. Regular review meetings and exception escalation are useful during transition because changes in demand, supplier reliability, or the bottleneck schedule can quickly affect material availability.
Study instruction:
- "Map the handoffs among production planning, inventory control, purchasing, and suppliers, including who updates and approves each schedule."
Key point:
- Batch-size policy crosses departmental boundaries.
- Shared schedules and clear ownership are necessary for reliable replenishment.
28. Q: Why does the chapter expect faster turnaround to improve customer service?
A: Show answer
When parts move through the plant more quickly and spend less time waiting in piles, the plant can complete orders sooner. Customers benefit because they receive products earlier and can plan their own operations with less uncertainty. Faster turnaround can also make the supplier more attractive when competitors require longer delivery periods. The chapter links smaller batches to shorter lead times, faster response, and a stronger marketplace position. The benefit depends on the plant actually meeting the new delivery commitment, not merely announcing a shorter lead time.
Study instruction:
- "Identify how a shorter and more reliable delivery cycle would affect a customer's planning, inventory, or ability to serve its own market."
Key point:
- Shorter production lead time can become a customer-service advantage.
- The promise must be supported by actual delivery performance.
29. Q: How can shorter lead times improve the plant's ability to respond to market changes?
A: Show answer
A shorter production cycle reduces the time between receiving an order and being able to ship it. This gives the plant more flexibility to respond to changes in customer requirements, order timing, and market demand. Faster response may help customers choose the plant over competitors whose delivery cycles are longer. It can also reduce the period during which forecasts and assumptions must remain accurate. The chapter treats responsiveness as a competitive advantage that can attract more orders, but the plant must preserve capacity and scheduling discipline as demand increases.
Study instruction:
- "Compare the plant's former and proposed order-to-shipment cycles and identify which customer decisions become easier with the shorter cycle."
Key point:
- Lead-time reduction increases the speed of response to demand.
- Responsiveness creates value only when the operation can sustain its commitments.
30. Q: How can a production improvement translate into increased sales?
A: Show answer
If the plant can deliver reliably sooner than competitors, sales staff have a stronger offer to present to customers. The chapter's logic is that shorter turnaround can attract customers, generate additional orders, and increase sales. The causal chain requires conditions: the promised lead time must be credible, products must meet customer requirements, sales must find suitable demand, and the plant must have enough constraint capacity to fulfill orders. Increased orders should therefore be evaluated against throughput and delivery performance rather than treated as an automatic result of inventory reduction.
Study instruction:
- "Trace the chain from smaller batches to lead time, customer offer, order conversion, shipped volume, and realized sales."
Key point:
- Operational speed can support a stronger commercial proposition.
- Sales growth depends on both market demand and the plant's ability to deliver.
31. Q: What evidence does Alex use to persuade marketing that the plant can promise earlier delivery?
A: Show answer
Alex presents a current list of customer orders showing promised due dates, Ralph's expected shipment dates, and actual shipment dates. The comparison demonstrates that the plant has cleared its overdue backlog and can predict shipment timing to within roughly twenty-four hours. He also compares recent orders with orders from about a month earlier to show that average production lead time has fallen from roughly three to four months to about two months or less. The evidence is stronger than a general assurance because it links a specific forecast to actual performance.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare an order-level report that compares customer promise dates, current shipment forecasts, and actual shipment dates."
Key point:
- Credible delivery claims require order-level evidence.
- Forecast accuracy and actual shipment history support commercial confidence.
32. Q: Why is the ability to predict shipment dates within about twenty-four hours commercially important?
A: Show answer
Reliable shipment forecasts allow sales and marketing to make commitments with a clearer understanding of operational capability. They also help customer-facing staff communicate changes before a missed date becomes a surprise. In the chapter, Alex uses the close agreement between expected and actual shipment dates as evidence that the plant has become more predictable. Predictability is different from speed: a fast but unreliable operation may still damage customer trust. A dependable forecast makes shorter lead-time promises more credible and helps the organization manage customer expectations.
Study instruction:
- "Calculate forecast error for a sample of completed orders and identify whether the stated prediction accuracy is supported by records."
Key point:
- Reliable forecasts make delivery commitments more credible.
- Predictability and speed are related but distinct dimensions of service.
33. Q: How should the plant distinguish its current average lead time from a new customer promise?
A: Show answer
The current average described in the chapter is about two months or less, following a reduction from roughly three to four months. A proposed four-week operating target is an additional improvement, not a result already proven across all orders. The team estimates that halving batches could reduce a six-to-eight-week production cycle to around four weeks, with some orders potentially taking three. Management should distinguish historical averages, tested capability, internal targets, and external commitments. Combining them into one figure can lead to overpromising and damage credibility.
Study instruction:
- "Label each lead-time figure as historical actual, current forecast, pilot result, internal target, or external promise."
Key point:
- Historical performance and future targets are not interchangeable.
- Customer commitments should reflect validated capability, not optimism alone.
34. Q: Why does Bob challenge the proposal to promise delivery in three weeks?
A: Show answer
Bob recognizes that a projected reduction is not the same as a proven delivery capability for every order. The plant's estimated results vary, and the new batch policy has not yet been demonstrated across all relevant products and conditions. Stacey also resists an aggressive commitment, while Lou is more willing to test the opportunity. Their disagreement highlights the tension between using improved capacity commercially and protecting company credibility. A responsible promise must account for product mix, order size, bottleneck load, material availability, and the reliability of the assumptions behind the estimate.
Study instruction:
- "Review a proposed delivery promise and identify the evidence and operational conditions that would justify it for different order types."
Key point:
- A forecasted best case should not automatically become a universal promise.
- Commercial ambition must be balanced with delivery risk.
35. Q: Why does Johnny Jons initially resist the proposed four-week delivery commitment?
A: Show answer
Jons remembers that the plant previously promised four months when demand was weak but sometimes took six months to deliver. That history makes a four-week claim appear implausible, even though current performance has improved. His concern is not only whether production can move faster but also what happens to customer and company credibility if the promise is missed. Alex must demonstrate that the operating system has changed and that the new commitment rests on current evidence rather than a sales slogan.
Study instruction:
- "Identify the historical service failures a customer-facing manager would reasonably consider before accepting a new lead-time claim."
Key point:
- Past delivery failures shape how customers and sales leaders assess new promises.
- Credibility must be rebuilt through evidence and consistent performance.
36. Q: Why does Jons agree to advertise a six-week factory-shipment term rather than the four weeks Alex requests?
A: Show answer
Jons accepts a more conservative six-week term after hearing Alex's evidence and confidence, rather than immediately adopting the four-week target. This creates a commercial opportunity while retaining some protection against uncertainty in the new operating approach. Jons also offers a personal wager if the plant ships new orders in less than five weeks, but the business point is the distinction between a market-facing commitment and a more ambitious internal capability. The six-week term gives sales a defined offer without claiming that every order will be completed in four weeks.
Study instruction:
- "Compare the proposed internal target with the external delivery term and explain why a controlled gap may protect credibility."
Key point:
- A conservative external promise can coexist with a more ambitious internal target.
- The promise should be both attractive and supportable.
37. Q: How should an organization manage the risk of promising a delivery time before the new process is fully proven?
A: Show answer
It should use recent order data, product-specific capacity checks, supplier confirmations, bottleneck schedules, and explicit assumptions before authorizing the promise. A limited offer or pilot can test the new commitment while the organization tracks actual shipment performance. Sales staff need clear rules for exceptions, order acceptance, and escalation when a product mix or workload falls outside the validated range. Management should avoid allowing incentives or enthusiasm to override operational evidence. If the plant misses a commitment, it should communicate early, investigate the cause, and revise the promise process.
Study instruction:
- "Draft a delivery-promise approval checklist that includes capacity, materials, product mix, forecast confidence, and exception authority."
Key point:
- Delivery promises require operational validation and controlled authorization.
- Early exception communication protects trust when assumptions change.
38. Q: What role does cross-functional collaboration play in the batch-size improvement?
A: Show answer
The proposal affects inventory control, production, purchasing, marketing, and sales. Stacey identifies inventory and supplier implications; Bob raises setup and labor concerns; Ralph contributes shipment forecasting; Lou recognizes the customer and sales opportunity; and Alex coordinates the overall decision. No single department can realize the full benefit independently. Operations may change batch sizes, but purchasing must adjust replenishment and marketing must communicate a credible offer. Cross-functional agreement aligns local decisions with the intended system result.
Study instruction:
- "Create a responsibility map for the batch-size change showing who proposes, approves, executes, monitors, and communicates each action."
Key point:
- The improvement depends on coordinated decisions across functions.
- Functional concerns should be resolved against shared system objectives.
39. Q: How should managers handle disagreement about the costs and benefits of smaller batches?
A: Show answer
They should make competing assumptions visible and test them against the plant's actual constraints. Bob focuses on increased setups and direct labor; Stacey identifies inventory and cash benefits; Alex explains idle non-bottleneck capacity; and the team considers faster delivery and sales. A useful decision process quantifies setup hours, available slack, inventory, lead time, bottleneck impact, and service outcomes. It should not dismiss local costs, but it should prevent those costs from being evaluated without the benefits and constraints of the entire system.
Study instruction:
- "Facilitate a decision review in which each function states its concern, supporting evidence, system impact, and proposed control."
Key point:
- Constructive challenge improves the quality of operational decisions.
- Compare local costs with system-wide effects using evidence.
40. Q: What risks could arise if smaller batches are introduced without adequate control?
A: Show answer
The plant could experience excessive setup workload, missing components, fragmented scheduling, additional handling, tracking errors, or interruptions to bottleneck supply. Suppliers may fail to meet more frequent deliveries, and assembly may wait if component timing becomes less synchronized. A poorly controlled change could also create misleading inventory figures or cause sales to promise lead times the operation cannot meet. These risks do not invalidate smaller batches; they show why the change must be linked to capacity planning, supplier coordination, material control, order visibility, and regular performance review.
Study instruction:
- "Build a risk register for the transition and assign a preventive control, warning indicator, owner, and response for each material risk."
Key point:
- Smaller batches require disciplined scheduling and material coordination.
- The improvement can fail if setup, supply, tracking, or promise controls are neglected.
41. Q: How can the plant tell whether additional setups are consuming only idle time or harming the constraint?
A: Show answer
It must identify where each setup occurs and compare the required setup workload with the resource's available capacity and schedule. The chapter's argument applies to non-bottlenecks that have idle time after material release is synchronized. It should not be generalized to a bottleneck, where additional setup can remove time from the resource that governs throughput. Managers should track setup duration, constraint availability, queue growth, starvation, and completion of required components. If the new setup pattern delays bottleneck work or downstream assembly, the batch policy needs adjustment.
Study instruction:
- "Separate setup records by resource and classify each resource as a current constraint or non-constraint before evaluating the effect."
Key point:
- The same setup increase can have very different consequences at different resources.
- Protect bottleneck time while using non-bottleneck slack intelligently.
42. Q: How does the plant's material-release rule support smaller batches?
A: Show answer
The plant has begun withholding materials from the floor until bottlenecks are ready for them. This prevents non-bottlenecks from producing far ahead of the constrained schedule and accumulating unnecessary work-in-process. With less premature release, non-bottlenecks have idle capacity that can absorb more frequent setups associated with smaller batches. The rule connects material release to the constraint's readiness rather than allowing every department to start work simply because material is available. Smaller batches are more effective when release discipline prevents excess work from entering the system.
Study instruction:
- "Review material-release signals and confirm that work is launched according to bottleneck readiness rather than local machine availability."
Key point:
- Controlled release limits premature work-in-process.
- Smaller batches work best when synchronized with the constraint.
43. Q: Why is reducing queue and wait time a better improvement target than merely reducing machine cycle time?
A: Show answer
Machine cycle time measures how long a resource takes to perform an operation, while queue and wait capture delays that may dominate a part's total elapsed time. If a part spends only a small fraction of its time being processed, a modest cycle-time improvement may barely affect its overall lead time. By contrast, reducing the time it waits for a bottleneck or a matching component can substantially shorten the production journey. The chapter encourages managers to examine where elapsed time is actually spent and direct effort toward the delays that control flow.
Study instruction:
- "For one product, rank the four elapsed-time elements by their contribution to total lead time and identify the largest improvement opportunity."
Key point:
- Improve the largest causes of elapsed time, not just the most visible machine activity.
- Queue and wait reductions can produce larger lead-time gains than isolated cycle-time changes.
44. Q: How can the plant avoid confusing lower work-in-process with lower throughput?
A: Show answer
Lower work-in-process is desirable only if the plant continues to meet demand and does not starve the bottleneck or delay assembly. Inventory reduction should be evaluated alongside completed output, shipment volume, due-date performance, and constraint availability. If inventory falls because materials are unavailable, throughput and customer service may deteriorate. If inventory falls because smaller batches move more quickly through a synchronized system, the change can improve both working capital and responsiveness. The distinction depends on the cause of the reduction, not the inventory number alone.
Study instruction:
- "Pair every inventory measure with throughput and delivery indicators and investigate any period when stock falls while output or service worsens."
Key point:
- Inventory reduction is not a success if it undermines flow.
- Assess inventory, throughput, and service together.
45. Q: How should management evaluate whether the new delivery offer is attracting profitable business?
A: Show answer
Management should track the number and value of orders won under the new delivery term, product mix, actual shipment time, contribution to throughput, and costs incurred to fulfill the orders. Faster delivery may attract additional demand, but not every order necessarily uses capacity in a way that benefits the system. Orders that overload the bottleneck or require unusual setups may affect other commitments. The chapter links speed with sales opportunity; a sound evaluation checks whether new sales can be fulfilled reliably and contribute to the plant's financial objective.
Study instruction:
- "Compare orders won under the revised delivery offer with their actual constraint usage, shipment reliability, and financial contribution."
Key point:
- Measure commercial gains through orders actually won and fulfilled.
- New demand must be evaluated against bottleneck capacity and economic value.
46. Q: What is the difference between improving the plant's internal lead time and changing the customer's total delivery experience?
A: Show answer
The chapter focuses on time spent inside the plant and on the period from customer contract to factory shipment. A customer's complete experience may also include order clarification, engineering approval, transport, installation, or other activities outside the production route. Reducing internal lead time is a major lever, but it does not automatically eliminate delays elsewhere. Sales and operations should define what the promise covers, such as factory shipment rather than delivery to the customer's site, and communicate that boundary clearly to avoid misunderstanding.
Study instruction:
- "Document the start and end points covered by the delivery promise and identify customer-facing activities outside that interval."
Key point:
- Internal production lead time is only one part of the customer's total elapsed time.
- Specify whether a commitment refers to factory shipment or final customer delivery.
47. Q: How can order-level records create a feedback loop between sales and production?
A: Show answer
Order records that compare promised dates, forecast shipment dates, and actual shipment dates allow sales and production to test whether commitments match operating capability. Production can use the records to improve planning and identify recurring sources of delay. Sales can use them to communicate realistic terms and identify which products or order types are consistently reliable. When forecast errors occur, the teams can review the cause and update assumptions. This turns delivery performance into shared information rather than a dispute between departments about who made an unrealistic promise.
Study instruction:
- "Establish a recurring review of forecast-versus-actual shipment dates and assign joint ownership to sales and production."
Key point:
- Shared order data connects commercial promises with operational performance.
- Forecast errors should lead to learning and updated assumptions.
48. Q: What should happen if supplier delivery frequency cannot be increased as planned?
A: Show answer
The plant should identify affected materials, how much buffer is genuinely needed, and whether alternative arrangements are feasible. Options may include phased delivery changes, supplier-managed stock, revised order quantities for selected items, or a different replenishment schedule for critical components. The plant should not reduce safety stock indiscriminately if supplier unreliability could starve a bottleneck. Purchasing should escalate commercial or capacity constraints and agree on a temporary control while the longer-term arrangement is negotiated. The objective is to preserve flow while avoiding unnecessary inventory.
Study instruction:
- "Select a supplier that cannot meet the proposed cadence and prepare a contingency plan that protects constraint availability."
Key point:
- Inventory targets must reflect actual supply reliability.
- A phased or alternative replenishment arrangement may be safer than a forced reduction.
49. Q: How can a plant distinguish a genuine system improvement from a temporary favorable period?
A: Show answer
It should compare performance across enough orders and operating conditions to account for product mix, demand changes, supplier reliability, and unusual disruptions. The chapter provides recent shipment evidence and a proposed next step, but a sustainable conclusion requires repeated results. Managers should monitor whether shorter lead times persist, whether work-in-process remains controlled, whether bottleneck output is protected, and whether on-time shipment is maintained as new orders arrive. A single successful week may reflect favorable circumstances; a repeatable process is stronger evidence of enduring improvement.
Study instruction:
- "Set a review horizon and compare performance by product family and workload level rather than relying on one aggregate period."
Key point:
- Sustained performance is stronger evidence than a short-lived improvement.
- Test the process under varying demand and operating conditions.
50. Q: What management decisions are needed before scaling the smaller-batch approach across the plant?
A: Show answer
Management should confirm that the pilot improves flow, identify product routes where the logic applies, and determine whether bottleneck schedules, setup capacity, supplier arrangements, and tracking systems can support wider use. It should define who may authorize exceptions, how batch quantities are updated, and how results will be reviewed. The organization should also ensure that marketing and sales commitments remain aligned with demonstrated capability. Scaling should follow evidence and readiness, not simply the desire to replicate a headline percentage reduction.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a scale-up decision paper covering validated results, affected products, resource capacity, supplier readiness, ownership, and unresolved risks."
Key point:
- Scale only after operating conditions and benefits are validated.
- Standardize controls and responsibilities before expanding the change.
51. Q: What is the central relationship among batch size, inventory, lead time, and market responsiveness?
A: Show answer
Smaller batches can reduce the amount of work accumulated between operations and allow parts to move forward sooner. Lower queue and wait time can shorten the period materials spend inside the plant, reducing work-in-process and potentially releasing cash. Shorter production lead time can improve order turnaround and enable the organization to respond to customers faster. If the plant can sustain the new performance, marketing gains a stronger delivery proposition and sales may increase. These outcomes form a connected chain; none should be assumed from batch size alone without confirming that bottlenecks, suppliers, and assembly remain synchronized.
Study instruction:
- "Draw a cause-and-effect map from batch size through queue, wait, inventory, lead time, delivery reliability, and market response."
Key point:
- Batch size is an operating lever with inventory, flow, and commercial consequences.
- The benefits depend on coordinated execution across the system.
52. Q: What are the most important lessons to retain from this chapter?
A: Show answer
The chapter argues that reducing non-bottleneck batch sizes can be the next logical step after improving bottleneck performance and controlling material release. Total time in the plant must be understood as setup, process, queue, and wait; queue and wait can dominate elapsed time. Bottlenecks shape throughput and inventory, so local setup savings at non-bottlenecks may be a mirage when they merely replace idle time. Smaller batches can reduce work-in-process, cash tied up, and lead time, while enabling faster customer response. The commercial opportunity must be supported by order-level evidence and a delivery promise the plant can reliably meet.
Study instruction:
- "Summarize the chapter's logic in a one-page flow diagram and use a real product route to demonstrate each link from batch size to customer delivery."
Key point:
- Manage flow around the constraint, not isolated machine efficiency.
- Convert verified operating improvements into credible customer value.
Rows: 52
Table 27
The Goal: Flow Improvement, Cost Measurement, and Customer Commitments
1. Q: What operational improvements does the chapter report after the plant changed its material-release and batch-size practices?
A: Show answer
The plant reports several connected improvements: new customer orders are being won, throughput has increased, inventories have fallen to their lowest level, and work is moving more smoothly between work centres. The initial release-control change limited the release of new materials until work at the heat-treat and NCX-10 constraints had progressed. Later, smaller batches reduced the time parts waited before moving to the next operation. These changes allowed the plant to ship accumulated finished goods without replacing them with unnecessary work-in-process. The evidence is a system-level improvement rather than a simple increase in the utilization of every machine.
Study instruction:
- "List the reported changes in throughput, inventory, flow, efficiencies, and customer orders, then explain how they reinforce one another."
Key point:
- The improvement is visible in system flow and shipped output, not merely local activity.
- Lower work-in-process can coexist with higher throughput when releases and transfers are controlled.
2. Q: How did controlled material release and smaller batches improve the movement of work through the plant?
A: Show answer
Controlled release prevented the plant from continually adding work faster than the constrained resources could process it. Smaller batches then allowed completed portions of work to move downstream earlier instead of waiting for an entire large batch to finish. Together, these practices reduced queues and shortened the time that jobs spent waiting between operations. They also made it easier to synchronize upstream release with the actual pace of the constraints. The result was a more continuous flow of work, less excess inventory on the floor, and a better chance of completing orders in time for shipment.
Study instruction:
- "Draw a simple process flow showing release, constraint processing, transfer to the next work centre, and shipment; mark where waiting is reduced."
Key point:
- Release control limits excess work entering the system.
- Smaller transfer quantities reduce waiting between operations.
3. Q: Why can a non-bottleneck work centre become a temporary bottleneck even when the plant has excess inventory?
A: Show answer
A non-bottleneck can temporarily restrict downstream flow when its output is held until a large batch is complete. The downstream centre may have no parts available even though many other items are waiting elsewhere in the plant. The constraint is then not the machine's long-run capacity but the timing and size of the transfer batch. The chapter describes work centres becoming idle while waiting for an upstream batch to finish. Smaller transfer quantities allow completed portions to move earlier and prevent batch-completion rules from creating avoidable local starvation.
Study instruction:
- "Identify a process where a downstream station waits for a complete batch and calculate how partial transfers could change its waiting pattern."
Key point:
- A temporary bottleneck can be created by release and transfer rules, not only by insufficient machine capacity.
- Inventory in the wrong location does not protect a downstream operation from starvation.
4. Q: Why is occasional idle time at a non-bottleneck not necessarily evidence of poor plant performance?
A: Show answer
A non-bottleneck has more capacity than the system needs from it at a particular moment. Keeping it busy for its own sake can create excess work-in-process, increase handling, and overload downstream stages. Its available time should be used when work is needed to support the system constraint, not simply to maximize a local utilization percentage. The chapter challenges the assumption that every worker must be continuously occupied. A short planned wait at a non-bottleneck may be economically preferable to producing parts that cannot yet contribute to a customer shipment.
Study instruction:
- "Compare a fully utilized non-bottleneck that creates excess inventory with a deliberately idle one that releases only what the system needs."
Key point:
- Local utilization is not the same as total-system productivity.
- Non-bottleneck capacity should be subordinated to the needs of the constraint.
5. Q: Why did smaller batches make idle time less disruptive to employees even though some waiting remained?
A: Show answer
Before the change, a work centre could wait for hours while an upstream centre completed a large batch. After the batches were reduced, waiting was divided into shorter intervals, often only several ten-to-twenty-minute periods during the day. The total amount of necessary idle time did not have to disappear for the workday to feel more balanced. Shorter interruptions made work appear to flow more regularly and reduced the conspicuous periods when people had nothing to process. This is an operational and human benefit, although it should not be confused with proof that every resource is optimally utilized.
Study instruction:
- "Map the timing of one operator's work before and after a batch-size reduction and distinguish total waiting from the length of each interruption."
Key point:
- The pattern of waiting matters as well as its total duration.
- Smoother flow can improve the work experience without requiring 100% utilization.
6. Q: What does the plant's reduction in work-in-process inventory indicate about its operating system?
A: Show answer
The reduction indicates that less work is being released and accumulated ahead of actual demand. The plant has shipped much of its excess finished inventory and has not refilled the floor with unnecessary work-in-process. The remaining work-in-process is described as being for current demand. This suggests that production release is becoming more closely connected to the system's ability to process and ship orders. Lower inventory can reduce congestion, handling, storage needs, and the time required to identify problems, but the chapter's key evidence is that inventory fell while throughput and customer activity improved.
Study instruction:
- "Separate inventory into raw materials, work-in-process, and finished goods, then identify which categories are excess and which support current demand."
Key point:
- Inventory should support flow and demand rather than conceal poor synchronization.
- A reduction in inventory is meaningful when it accompanies maintained or improved delivery performance.
7. Q: How should managers evaluate the combined effect of throughput, inventory, and operating expense?
A: Show answer
Managers should assess whether the organization is generating more money through sales while reducing the amount of money tied up in inventory and controlling the expense of operating the system. The chapter contrasts this system view with a narrow unit-cost calculation that rises when setup time is allocated across smaller batches. A single metric can give a misleading signal if it ignores the effects on total output, inventory, and actual expense. Managers should therefore examine the direction and relationship of the measures together, while retaining appropriate financial records for external reporting and internal accountability.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a three-measure review using throughput, inventory, and operating expense; explain what a simultaneous improvement in all three would mean."
Key point:
- A system-level decision should be judged by its effect on the whole operation.
- No isolated cost or efficiency measure should override evidence about total performance.
8. Q: Why can conventional efficiency measurements conflict with the objective of improving overall flow?
A: Show answer
Conventional efficiency measures often reward individual resources for staying busy and spreading allocated costs over as many units as possible. That can encourage large batches, premature production, and excess inventory even when those actions do not increase shipments. The chapter shows that a non-bottleneck may be deliberately idle while the plant is better off overall. It also shows that smaller batches can raise the calculated labour minutes per part because setup time is divided across fewer units. A measurement system that treats these effects as deterioration may discourage changes that improve throughput and reduce inventory.
Study instruction:
- "Find an efficiency measure in a manufacturing report and identify behaviours it may encourage that do not necessarily improve customer delivery or system throughput."
Key point:
- A measure can be internally consistent yet still encourage counterproductive decisions.
- Performance indicators must reflect the purpose of the system they are intended to manage.
9. Q: How does reducing a production batch from 100 parts to 50 parts change the setup time allocated to each part in the chapter's example?
A: Show answer
The example assumes a two-hour setup, or 120 minutes, and five minutes of processing per part. With 100 parts, the setup allocation is 120 divided by 100, or 1.2 minutes per part; the calculated direct-labour time is therefore 6.2 minutes per part. With 50 parts, the same 120-minute setup is divided by only 50 units, producing 2.4 setup minutes per part and a calculated total of 7.4 minutes. The setup event has not become longer; only the allocation per unit has increased because the batch contains fewer units.
Study instruction:
- "Recalculate the example for batch sizes of 100, 50, and 25, keeping setup time and processing time constant."
Key point:
- Setup allocation per unit rises as batch quantity falls when setup duration is unchanged.
- A higher allocated time per unit does not by itself prove that actual resource spending increased.
10. Q: Why does the calculated unit cost rise when the same setup time is spread over a smaller batch?
A: Show answer
The allocation formula divides a fixed setup duration by the number of units in the batch. Halving the batch size therefore doubles the setup minutes assigned to each unit, even though the machine still performs one setup of the same duration. If the cost model converts those allocated minutes into direct labour cost and then applies a burden factor, the calculated burden also rises. This is a mathematical consequence of the allocation method. It describes how the accounting model assigns cost to units; it does not establish that the organization has hired more people or incurred an equivalent increase in cash expenditure.
Study instruction:
- "Explain the difference between a change in an allocation denominator and a change in the underlying resource consumption."
Key point:
- The cost increase in the example is driven by allocation across fewer units.
- Allocation effects must be distinguished from incremental cash or capacity costs.
11. Q: Does a higher calculated direct-labour cost per part prove that the plant's actual operating expenses have increased?
A: Show answer
No. In the chapter, the plant has not added employees to the payroll, and the additional setups do not automatically create additional payroll or other operating expense. The reported unit cost rises because the accounting model allocates setup time over smaller quantities and calculates burden as a factor of direct labour. Actual expense must be examined through payroll, supplier charges, energy, maintenance, overtime, freight, and other real resource costs. If those expenses remain stable while more saleable output is produced, the cost per unit of output may fall even though the allocated labour minutes per part rise.
Study instruction:
- "For a proposed process change, list the actual expense categories that could change and separate them from costs that merely move between unit-cost allocations."
Key point:
- A calculated unit cost is not the same thing as an actual expenditure.
- Validate cost conclusions against real resource consumption and total operating expense.
12. Q: How can the plant's actual cost per unit fall while the accounting calculation for direct labour per part rises?
A: Show answer
The plant can produce and sell more output with substantially the same workforce and operating-cost base. The additional setups increase the setup allocation assigned to each smaller batch, but the system's higher throughput spreads the overall operating expense across more saleable units. At the same time, lower inventory reduces the amount of money tied up in unsold production. The chapter therefore distinguishes a higher standard or allocated cost for an individual part from improved economics for the plant as a whole. The conclusion depends on actual volume, sales, resource spending, and delivery performance, not on the allocation figure alone.
Study instruction:
- "Build a simple before-and-after example with unchanged operating expense and higher shipped volume; calculate average operating expense per shipped unit."
Key point:
- More saleable throughput can improve average economics even when a unit allocation rises.
- Inventory reduction and cash-generating shipments are part of the economic evaluation.
13. Q: What assumption in the plant's cost measurement makes the smaller-batch change appear more expensive than it really is?
A: Show answer
The measurement assumes that workers are fully occupied all the time. Under that assumption, additional setup work appears to require additional labour capacity because no unused time is available to absorb it. The chapter rejects this assumption for the plant's actual conditions: non-bottlenecks have idle periods, and the existing workforce can perform additional setups without an automatic increase in headcount. A sound analysis must therefore consider available capacity and the constraint's workload rather than treating every minute of every employee as already committed to productive work.
Study instruction:
- "Test the full-utilization assumption by reviewing actual labour schedules, idle periods, overtime, staffing levels, and constraint utilization."
Key point:
- A costing model's assumptions must be checked against the operating reality.
- Unused capacity can absorb some additional activity without creating equivalent incremental payroll.
14. Q: How should managers distinguish a product-cost allocation from the incremental cost of accepting a process change?
A: Show answer
A product-cost allocation assigns existing or shared costs to units according to a chosen rule. Incremental cost asks what additional resources the decision will actually require compared with the alternative. For smaller batches, managers should identify extra setup hours, any overtime, additional consumables, maintenance, handling, transport, or quality costs, and determine which of those are genuinely incremental. They should not infer an incremental expense solely from a higher allocated labour figure. Conversely, they must not dismiss real extra costs simply because payroll has not changed. Both views are useful, but they answer different management questions.
Study instruction:
- "For a batch-size proposal, prepare two columns: accounting allocation changes and incremental resource changes; support each item with evidence."
Key point:
- Allocation answers how costs are assigned; incremental analysis asks what the decision adds.
- A credible business case identifies both benefits and genuine additional resource requirements.
15. Q: What is the difference between a transfer batch and a process batch, and why does the distinction matter here?
A: Show answer
A process batch is the quantity treated together during an operation, while a transfer batch is the quantity moved to the next operation at one time. The chapter's problem arose because materials handlers often waited for the entire upstream batch to finish before moving any parts. Reducing batch sizes helped the plant move work sooner, but the deeper operational distinction is that a process need not always wait for every unit in a batch to complete before downstream work begins. Separating these quantities can reduce waiting and lead time, provided the process, quality, handling, and traceability requirements permit partial transfers.
Study instruction:
- "Take one product route and mark the process quantity and transfer quantity at each step; identify where partial transfer is technically and economically practical."
Key point:
- The amount processed together need not always equal the amount transferred together.
- Smaller transfer quantities can improve flow without requiring every operation to change its technical method.
16. Q: Why did the plant initially experience a dip in reported efficiencies after controlling material releases?
A: Show answer
The plant was consuming excess inventory that had accumulated under the previous operating approach. Once the release of new materials was restricted and releases were synchronized with the completion of work at the constraints, some work centres had less material available to keep them busy. Local efficiency figures therefore fell temporarily. The chapter presents this dip as a transition effect rather than evidence that the system was deteriorating. After the excess inventory was exhausted and throughput increased, the reported efficiencies recovered. Managers should interpret temporary utilization changes in the context of inventory depletion and system performance.
Study instruction:
- "Construct a timeline showing the release-control change, consumption of excess inventory, temporary efficiency dip, and subsequent recovery."
Key point:
- A short-term efficiency decline can accompany removal of excess inventory.
- Transition effects should be assessed against throughput and delivery outcomes.
17. Q: How can smaller batches shorten production lead time without increasing the plant's total processing capacity?
A: Show answer
Smaller batches allow completed portions of an order to move to the next operation before the entire production lot is finished. This reduces the waiting time between work centres and allows downstream operations to begin sooner. The plant does not necessarily gain more machine hours or a higher physical processing rate at the bottleneck; it uses the available capacity with less delay and less work trapped in queues. Shorter lead time can make due dates easier to meet and can create flexibility for additional orders. The benefit depends on coordinated scheduling and timely availability of materials.
Study instruction:
- "Compare the elapsed time from first processing to shipment under full-batch transfer and partial-batch transfer, holding processing times constant."
Key point:
- Flow improvements can release capacity from waiting and queue time rather than from faster machines.
- Shorter lead time creates scheduling flexibility but does not automatically increase constraint capacity.
18. Q: What risks should managers examine before reducing batch sizes further?
A: Show answer
Smaller batches can increase the frequency of setups, scheduling transactions, material movements, inspections, and changeovers. If setup time is long, equipment is fragile, or a process requires a fixed minimum lot, excessive fragmentation may consume scarce capacity or increase defects and handling cost. The chapter's proposal is evaluated in the context of available bottleneck capacity and existing commitments, not adopted as a universal rule. Managers should pilot the change, measure actual setup duration and constraint load, verify quality and traceability, and compare the flow benefit with the additional work required to manage more frequent transfers and setups.
Study instruction:
- "Create a trial checklist covering setup time, constraint utilization, quality, handling, traceability, WIP, lead time, and on-time shipment."
Key point:
- Smaller batches are a flow lever, not an unconditional target.
- The right batch size balances waiting-time benefits with setup and handling consequences.
19. Q: Why is a system-level view necessary when judging whether the plant's improvements are successful?
A: Show answer
A system-level view asks whether the plant can turn customer demand into completed shipments with less inventory and controlled operating expense. Local measures may reward activity that creates no additional saleable output, while a constraint may determine the pace of the whole system. The chapter shows that lower local utilization, higher allocated setup time, and more frequent setups can coexist with smoother flow, higher throughput, and lower inventory. Managers must therefore evaluate the combined effect on the plant's purpose rather than optimizing each department independently.
Study instruction:
- "Choose one local performance indicator and explain how improving it could worsen throughput, inventory, or delivery elsewhere in the system."
Key point:
- The performance of the whole plant is more important than isolated departmental scores.
- Measures should support decisions that improve system throughput and delivery reliability.
20. Q: Why is Lou's suggestion to change the costing base from twelve months to two months ethically and procedurally risky?
A: Show answer
Lou proposes using a recent two-month period because throughput has improved, even though the applicable accounting policy calls for a twelve-month base. He acknowledges that the alternative is not valid under the policy and suggests that the change might pass an initial review but fail if division personnel investigate. That turns a legitimate concern about a misleading cost signal into a proposal to conceal a non-compliant method. The risk includes inaccurate reporting, loss of management credibility, audit findings, and potentially serious consequences for the people who approve or rely on the figures. A favourable result does not make an unsupported method acceptable.
Study instruction:
- "Identify the stated policy, the proposed departure, who would rely on the report, and the evidence that would be needed to justify any formal policy change."
Key point:
- A reporting method should not be altered secretly to obtain a favourable result.
- Transparency and policy compliance protect the credibility of operational improvements.
21. Q: How should managers respond when an approved costing method produces a signal that conflicts with actual operating improvement?
A: Show answer
Managers should preserve the required accounting method, explain its assumptions, and supplement it with clearly labelled operational analysis. They can reconcile the reported unit-cost movement to setup allocation, batch size, actual payroll, total operating expense, throughput, and inventory. If the method is genuinely unsuitable for the changed operation, the issue should be raised through the formal accounting-policy or management-reporting governance process, with documented rationale and approval before implementation. The response should not be to disguise a non-compliant calculation. Decision-makers need both reliable formal reporting and transparent operational measures to understand the plant's performance.
Study instruction:
- "Draft a reconciliation that explains the calculated unit-cost increase while separately reporting actual expense, throughput, inventory, and shipment trends."
Key point:
- Explain the limitation of a metric without falsifying or silently changing it.
- Any change to a formal costing policy requires proper authorization and disclosure.
22. Q: What is the difference between a representative recent cost period and a policy-compliant costing period?
A: Show answer
A recent period may better reflect current operating conditions after a major process change, but representativeness alone does not authorize its use in a formal calculation. A prescribed twelve-month base may be intended to smooth volatility or satisfy a consistent policy. A two-month period could be useful as a supplemental management analysis if it is clearly identified, consistently calculated, and not presented as the required formal measure. Whether the official basis can be changed depends on the organization's accounting policy and governance. Managers must distinguish analytical usefulness from permission to change an approved reporting method.
Study instruction:
- "Compare the purpose, calculation, approval status, and intended users of the formal twelve-month measure and any supplemental recent-period analysis."
Key point:
- A useful management indicator is not automatically a valid replacement for a prescribed accounting measure.
- Label alternative analyses clearly and retain the approved basis for formal reporting.
23. Q: What information should management present to explain why the smaller-batch strategy improves the plant despite higher allocated part costs?
A: Show answer
Management should show the setup-time allocation mechanics and explain that the same setup duration is spread over fewer units. It should then present actual staffing and payroll, any other incremental setup costs, total operating expense, throughput, work-in-process, finished-goods inventory, and on-time shipments. A before-and-after comparison should use consistent definitions and disclose the period covered. It should also identify the constraint's workload and show whether the plant is meeting existing customer commitments. This combination allows reviewers to distinguish a change in cost assignment from a real deterioration in resource economics or operating performance.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a one-page management bridge from allocated unit cost to actual expense and system results, with consistent periods and definitions."
Key point:
- A transparent bridge is more persuasive than selectively presenting a favourable metric.
- Operational evidence should explain, not replace, reliable financial information.
24. Q: What should a manager do when a senior reviewer may misunderstand an unfavourable cost indicator?
A: Show answer
The manager should anticipate the likely interpretation and provide a concise, evidence-based explanation before the indicator is used to judge performance. The explanation should state what changed, why the calculation moved, which assumptions are affected, and what independent measures show about actual results. Supporting schedules should be available for review, and any policy limitation should be disclosed rather than hidden. If the reviewer still disagrees, the issue should be escalated through the appropriate management and finance channels. The chapter's tension demonstrates why communication about measurement design is part of change management.
Study instruction:
- "Prepare a briefing that explains the cost movement in plain language and includes evidence a reviewer could independently verify."
Key point:
- Do not allow an unexplained metric to define the narrative of an operational change.
- Credibility depends on openness about both favourable results and measurement limitations.
25. Q: Why is accepting Burnside's order for 1,000 Model 12 units in two weeks not simply a sales decision?
A: Show answer
The order would generate more than a million dollars in sales, but it would also consume bottleneck capacity, require sufficient electronic control modules, and affect the schedule of existing customers. The plant initially has only about 50 finished units available and would need to manufacture the remaining 950. A sales decision becomes an operations decision when the promised quantity and date depend on constrained resources, material lead times, and shipping arrangements. The order must be evaluated against the whole production system and the plant's ability to make a credible commitment, not accepted solely because the revenue figure is attractive.
Study instruction:
- "List the capacity, material, schedule, customer, and logistics checks that must precede acceptance of an urgent order."
Key point:
- Revenue opportunity must be tested against operational feasibility.
- A customer promise is only valuable if the plant can reliably fulfil it.
26. Q: Why was the initial estimate of about 100 Model 12 units per day insufficient to justify a two-week commitment?
A: Show answer
The bottlenecks could produce Model 12 parts at about 100 units per day, but the estimate assumed the plant would work on nothing else for two weeks. That would displace existing orders and could damage relationships with many customers. The rate also does not, by itself, prove that materials, subassemblies, labour, inspection, and shipping are ready at the same pace. Capacity must be evaluated as available constraint time after existing commitments, not as a gross daily rate that ignores the rest of the schedule.
Study instruction:
- "Convert the 100-units-per-day estimate into a capacity plan that deducts current bottleneck commitments and includes material and shipping dependencies."
Key point:
- Gross production rate is not the same as available-to-promise capacity.
- A plan that sacrifices existing customer commitments may create more damage than the new order is worth.
27. Q: How should the bottleneck's production rate be used when evaluating a new customer order?
A: Show answer
The bottleneck rate provides a starting point for estimating the maximum pace at which the system can complete the constrained work. Managers must compare the required quantity with available bottleneck hours, current workload, product mix, setup requirements, downtime, and the sequence of existing orders. The estimate should then be checked against upstream material availability and downstream finishing and shipment capacity. In the chapter, the 100-units-per-day figure shows technical possibility only under a dedicated schedule. It does not establish that the full order can be added without consequences.
Study instruction:
